- Then `prek run --all-files`, with `yarn install` first if eslint is missing.
- Commit trailer: `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.

## The one defect
An audit (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-ha-builtin-audit.md`; read its finding on `get_locks_from_targets`) found that the `hard_refresh_usercodes` action resolves its targets with LCM's own `get_locks_from_targets` (`domain/locks.py`, around line 114) and a hand-built schema. The problems:
- An area target matches only locks whose ENTITY has that area. Most integrations put the area on the DEVICE, so targeting by area probably misses most locks.
- Floor, label and group targets aren't supported.
- Calls that mix target types are rejected.

The audit read an older main, so **first verify each claim against current main**, and read the existing test. If the defect isn't as described, STOP and report.

## The fix
- Resolve targets the way any HA entity service does:
  - `homeassistant.helpers.service.async_extract_entity_ids`, or the closest current HA API, e.g. `async_extract_referenced_entity_ids` / target selector helpers;
  - the standard `cv.ENTITY_SERVICE_FIELDS` / target schema.
- Then keep only lock entities that LCM manages, with the same filtering the current function applies after resolving.
- Read the venv's `homeassistant/helpers/service.py` to choose the right API for HA 2026.9.0, LCM's minimum.
- Keep the action's user-facing behavior otherwise the same:
  - same errors for no matching managed locks, if any exist today;
  - check `services.yaml` / `strings.json` for target definitions that need updating.
- Find every caller of `get_locks_from_targets`, and either migrate them all or keep the function as a thin wrapper over HA's helper. Pick the smaller correct change.

## Tests (each must fail on main first)
- Area set on the lock's DEVICE, not the entity: targeting that area refreshes the lock.
- Area on the entity: still works.
- Device target, and a label target or a mixed target: they resolve.
- A target that matches a lock LCM doesn't manage: the current behavior is unchanged.

## Scope discipline
- No other changes. List anything you notice in your report.
- One commit, e.g. `fix: resolve hard_refresh_usercodes targets like any entity service`.

## Report
- The SHA.
- What you verified against current main.
- The API you chose and why.
- Failing-first evidence.
- Suite, coverage and prek results.
- Anything noticed but left alone.

## Proposed change

Several Lock Code Manager configurations can share one physical lock. They share one lock instance and one coordinator. That coordinator used to be built with the configuration that created it, so Home Assistant shut it down when *that* configuration unloaded. Disabling or reloading the creating configuration stopped the coordinator for good while another configuration still used the lock: polls and refreshes did nothing, drift checks stopped, and writes were never confirmed. A reload of the creating configuration then picked up the same dead instance.

**The coordinator now belongs to no config entry.** It belongs to the lock instance, and Lock Code Manager's own teardown owns its lifetime.
- **First read:** always `async_refresh()`. Lock Code Manager already handled a failed first read itself and never relied on Home Assistant retrying the entry.
- **Teardown:** an instance is torn down when the last configuration holding it lets go. This is decided by **instance identity, in any state**, like a reference count. Joining a shared lock still considers only loaded configurations, and the docstring says why the two rules differ.
- **No double shutdown:** each lock is popped and checked for another holder in the same step, with no await in between. Two configurations unloading at the same moment tear a shared lock down once.
- **Failed setup:** a lock whose setup fails after its coordinator exists is shut down when dropped, unless another configuration holds the same instance.
- **After shutdown, nothing is recorded.** The coordinator's state-changing methods (backoff, backoff reset, applying a read, data updates) do nothing. So a poll, write, push or drift check that answers late can't raise a repair for a lock that's gone, or clear the repair of the lock set up in its place. This holds from shutdown, which is the last step of teardown.

**Known and accepted:**
- **FAILED_UNLOAD:** a configuration stuck in FAILED_UNLOAD keeps its instance alive.
- **"Disable polling":** a configuration's "Disable polling" system option no longer applies to these locks. Home Assistant reads it from a coordinator's own entry, and this one has none. A per-holder rule is left to a later redesign of shared-lock ownership.
- **Startup logging:** a lock that isn't ready at startup logs Home Assistant's refresh error as well as Lock Code Manager's info line. That was already the case for nearly every real setup.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [x] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: fixes #
- This PR is related to issue: #1623

**Tests** run through real setup, unload and reload of shared configurations:
- **Creating configuration disabled or reloaded:** the coordinator keeps working, and has no config entry. This failed on main.
- **Unload in either order:** shutdown happens exactly once. This failed on main.
- **Teardown and setup races:**
  - two configurations unloading at once;
  - a holder that is still unloading;
  - unloading while another configuration rebuilds the lock;
  - a failed setup next to an unloading instance.
- **Late answers after teardown** record nothing:
  - a poll failing or answering (an existing repair survives);
  - a write failure (the breaker is unchanged and no repair is raised);
  - a push (an existing repair survives).
- **A shared polled lock** keeps polling after the configuration that built it leaves.

Mutation checks show each test catches the defect it guards.

## Why this document exists

## Sources (read them)
- **Roadmap:** `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-08-credential-model-roadmap.md`. Use especially:

  - `feedback_release_must_invert_acquire.md`

- **Current code:** origin/main. Run `git -C /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager fetch -q origin`, then read with `git show origin/main:<path>`, or use a temporary `git worktree add` under `/private/tmp/claude-501/design-review-main` (remove it when done).

## The flaws (from the roadmap, numbered as there)
1. `data` mixes the lock's word with LCM's belief: optimistic pushes, given-up beliefs.
2. Two schedulers (the sync tick and the coordinator's confirmation look) hand verdicts across (`_failed_writes`) and race. Verdicts get lost or misattributed.

5. Pushes and events are treated as observations: retained MQTT replays, stale Matter events, the anchor fallback.

8. Transport quirks leak into the core.
9. There's no principled rule for what a lock's refusal does to a slot: disable (`CodeRejectedError`), suspend now (`LockOperationUnsupported`), breaker (`LockOperationFailed`), or success.

- **Interaction with the spec:** which spec decisions the refactors make easier, change, or make unnecessary. Flag any spec decision a flaw's evidence now contradicts.
- **Decisions for Raman:** a short numbered list of the choices that need him, each with your recommendation.

## Style
- Factual and cited. Don't claim behavior you didn't read in the code (memory: "no unsourced claims", "read the framework before claiming a limit").
- Spell out acronyms on first use.

The design review is ready at `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-coordinator-design-review.md`. It's about 600 lines, sized for a 20-minute read, and cites main at `963e0fb5`. I checked its most serious new claim against the code: the refused-clear loop is plausible (detail at the end).

**The flaws at a glance:**

| # | Flaw | Refactor | Before the model work? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `data` mixes the lock's word with LCM's belief | **R5** one in-memory belief owner, then spec PR B persists it | yes |
| 2 | Two schedulers hand verdicts across | Removed by E (no interim PR) | in E |
| 3 | Set/clear asymmetric | E's write contract | in E |
| 4 | Decisions made before the lock's turn | **R3** read scope and time budget decided once the turn is taken | yes |
| 5 | Pushes and events treated as observations | **R6** per-provider push fixes (zwave-js-ui, Matter, Z2M); ordering in E | partly |
| 6 | One concept, several definitions | **R1** named "manages" predicates; Matter readers (**R7**); "desired" in E | partly |
| 7 | Unreadable counts as present | E's `nothing` value | in E |
| 8 | Transport quirks leak into the core | No PR of its own; a checklist every PR must pass | — |
| 9 | No rule for what a refusal does to a slot | **R4** one refusal table | yes |
| 10 | Shared-lock ownership spread over three paths | **R2** one lock owner with explicit acquire/release | yes |
| **11 (new)** | Background work a lock starts has no owner; shutdown is a flag checked in each method | Folded into **R2** | yes |

**Proposed order:**
1. **Step 0:** a tiny bug fix: `get_entry_config` mustn't trust a failed setup's cache.
2. **The refactors, in order:** R1 → R2 (+ R2p, per-holder polling) → R3 → R4 → spec PR C → R5 → spec PR B → R6.
3. **Then E,** then F / #1581.

Spec PR D, R7 and the built-in audit cleanups fill the gaps. Each PR fixes one defect or one ownership and gets at most two review rounds.

**Seven decisions it needs from you,** with its recommendation for each:
1. **Refusal rule:** classify by "what would change the outcome". A refused *clear* never disables the slot; it suspends with a repair saying the code may still be on the lock.
2. **Per-holder "Disable polling":** poll unless every holder disabled it. Never suppress recovery probes, and re-check when holders join or leave (on top of R2).
3. **Flaw 2 until E:** accept the bounded "one strike lost" defect rather than build something E deletes.
4. **The order above.**
5. **What "managed" means for reads:** read scope covers slots of entries that keep their slots, plus any slot with a belief or pending write. "Is this slot anyone's" includes disabled entries.
6. **Release clears (#1622):** E gives them a judge. A code still on the lock after one retry raises a specific repair, and the unmanaged sweep runs on every read, not only at migration.
7. **"Desired" means what sync wants** (the active state). Handle #863 inside the providers, which retires `_expects_pin`.

**It also flags four places where the evidence contradicts or leaves gaps in the credential-model spec.** The main one: §3.3 "route exceptions exactly as today" would freeze the refused-clear loop.

**A probable bug, not yet reproduced.**
- **The code:** when a clear is refused with `CodeRejectedError` (`sync.py:939`), sync disables the slot and expects the next check to find "no code wanted, no code on the lock".
- **Why that loops:** a *refused* clear leaves the code on the lock, so the slot stays out of sync and the clear is retried every tick, uncharged. On main, a ZHA clear with a non-zero status raises exactly that error.
- **How it's fixed depends on decision 1.**

description: In this repo's HA test harness, the freezer fixture drives both time.monotonic and the event-loop clock; prefer it over hand-rolled clocks
metadata:

`pytest_homeassistant_custom_component`'s `patch_time.py` replaces
`runner.monotonic` with a freezegun-patchable function. As a result:

- **`freezer` drives both clocks.** `freezer.tick(...)` moves `time.monotonic()`
  AND the event loop's `loop.time()`, so it also moves `asyncio.sleep`.
- **A frozen loop clock stalls sleeps.** An `asyncio.sleep(d)` never completes
  until the test ticks at least `d` and lets the loop run.
- **Freezing jumps to wall time.** The clock jumps to epoch seconds (~1.79e9),
  so timers set before freezing fire on the next loop turn.
- **Step sizes matter.** Use steps that don't land exactly on a due time, or
  the float rounds either way. Bound every stepping loop and fail loudly:
  `hass.async_block_till_done()` on a frozen clock can spin forever, and
  pytest-timeout won't break it.
- **Reference implementation:** `tests/providers/test_base.py` on main (#1628):
  `_step_clock_until`, `_settle_background`, `paced_lock`.

Raman (2026-10-11) asked why a custom `RateLimitClock` was written instead
of HA's tools. Check the harness and HA's `util`/`helpers` before building
your own. The audit of that is
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-ha-builtin-audit.md`.

Related PR hygiene: edit a PR's body before pushing. Editing right after a
push starts a second Labeler run, and the cancelled run shows red in the PR
checks (#1628).

input.prompt:
Make ONE minimal bug fix in Lock Code Manager (LCM), a Home Assistant custom integration that syncs PIN codes to smart locks.

## Workspace (strict)
- Work ONLY in `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/failed-setup-config-cache`, branch `fix/failed-setup-config-cache` (fresh from origin/main 963e0fb5). Use absolute paths.
- No push, no amend, no bare `git stash`. Don't commit `.entire/.gitignore`.
- Mutation checks ONLY in an rsync copy under `/private/tmp/claude-501/config-cache-scratch/`, restoring in a `finally`.
- Follow `AGENTS.md`. Tests use real setup, failed setup and reload of config entries, never hand-built `runtime_data`.
- Tests: `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q -n auto --cov=custom_components/lock_code_manager --cov-report=term-missing:skip-covered` (100% coverage).
- Then `prek run --all-files`; run `yarn install` first if eslint is missing.
- Commit trailer: `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.

## The one defect
- `get_entry_config(entry)` returns `entry.runtime_data.config` when `runtime_data` exists; otherwise it rebuilds from the entry (`EntryConfig.from_entry`).
- Home Assistant does NOT delete `runtime_data` when setup fails. Unloading a non-LOADED entry doesn't delete it either.
- So once a setup fails after `runtime_data` was assigned (`__init__.py`, around the assignment in `async_setup_entry`), every later reader trusts a stale cached config instead of the stored data.
- PR #1630 fixed only setup's own missing-lock check, by switching it to `EntryConfig.from_entry`. These readers still see the stale cache on such an entry:
  - the options flow's form default and slot checks;
  - `_check_common_slots`;
  - `_lock_managed_by_other_entry`;
  - the managed-slot queries, when they look at a failed entry.
- Read the design review's section on this:
  - document: `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-coordinator-design-review.md`;
  - search for "Step 0" and for `get_entry_config`.

## The fix (minimal)
- Make `get_entry_config` trust `runtime_data.config` only when it can be current.
  - **Recommended rule:** the entry is LOADED, or setup is in progress after this run assigned fresh `runtime_data`. Otherwise rebuild from the entry.
- **Read first:** where `runtime_data` is assigned during setup, and which readers run during SETUP_IN_PROGRESS. A setup-time reader must still see the fresh config. Pick the rule that is correct for every state and say why.
  - If a simple state check can't tell "fresh this run" from "stale from a failed run", an alternative is to clear or replace `runtime_data` at the start of setup.
  - Choose the least invasive correct option.
- Once the general fix covers setup's own read, PR #1630's special case in `async_setup_entry` (`EntryConfig.from_entry` for the missing-lock check) may become redundant. Simplify it if so, and keep its test passing.
- Don't change anything else.

## Tests (each must fail on main first)
1. An entry whose setup failed after `runtime_data` was assigned. Change its stored data (e.g. via `async_update_entry`). Then `get_entry_config` reflects the stored data, not the stale cache.
2. A user-visible consequence. For example: the options flow's default locks, or another entry's overlap check, see the stored data for that failed entry.
3. Setup-time readers still see the fresh config, and a LOADED entry still uses its cache. Show that the cache is still the source by mutating it in a test, if needed.

## Scope discipline
- No other changes. List anything you notice in the report.
- One commit, e.g. `fix: don't trust a failed setup's cached config`.

## Report
- The SHA.
- The rule you chose and why it is correct in each state.
- Failing-first evidence.
- Suite, coverage and prek results.
- Anything noticed.

**What a ZHA lock that keeps refusing a clear does today:**
- **One clear per sync tick, forever:** 30 clears in 30 ticks.

- **The code stays on the lock,** and the slot reads out of sync.

**The fix is your decision 1 (the refusal rule).** The design review recommends that a refused clear never disables the slot, and instead suspends it with a repair saying the code may still be on the lock. Then the fixed `slot_suspended` description from `strings.json` (~425):
> "...will resume automatically once **the lock accepts the code** or you change the PIN..."

**Fix**

1. **Give the refused clear its own accurate text.**

3. **Tell the user how to get the code removed.** For example: remove the code at the lock (keypad or the lock's own app). Sync resumes once the lock reports the slot empty, or when this slot's PIN or active state changes. Say it once, accurately.

5. **Make the error log's resume rule match** (sync.py ~944): also "or once the lock reports the slot empty".

   - say the code may still be on the lock;
   - say how to remove it;
   - contain neither "cannot set code" nor a `<Status.` repr;
   - give one resume rule.

## Proposed change

When a lock refused to clear a slot's code (`CodeRejectedError` on a clear), sync **disabled** the slot. A disabled slot that still holds a code is out of sync, so the same clear was sent again on every tick, forever. Disabling also reset the slot breaker, so the failures were never counted and the slot never suspended. In a reproduction, a ZHA lock that refuses every clear got 30 clears in 30 ticks, with the code still on the lock. The user saw a "slot disabled, re-enable it" repair recreated every tick. It never said the code might still open the door. For a slot whose condition was off, the refusal also flipped the user's enabled switch off.

**What changes.** A refused clear now **suspends** the slot at once, through the existing suspension path, and never disables it. A refused set keeps today's behavior and still disables the slot.

**The repair** has its own wording. It keeps the same issue and acknowledge flow, under a new `slot_clear_failed` translation key. It says:
- Lock Code Manager couldn't remove the code, and gives the lock's reason, e.g. `status FAILURE (1)`;
- the code may still be on the lock and may still open the door, and to delete it at the lock (keypad or the lock maker's app);
- sync resumes once the lock reports the slot empty, or when this slot's PIN or active state changes.

`CodeRejectedError` now keeps the provider's `reason`, so this repair doesn't show the exception's "cannot set code" text. ZHA statuses show as `FAILURE (1)` instead of a Python enum repr.

In practice, only ZHA can trigger this. A non-zero status in a Clear PIN Code Response raises `CodeRejectedError`; other providers don't raise it on a clear.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [x] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: fixes #
- This PR is related to issue: #1627

**Tests** are ZHA end to end, on stock and quirk clusters, with three triggers (slot disabled, PIN emptied, condition off). They check:
- the clear is sent once and never again;
- the slot is suspended with a `slot_clear_failed` repair, and there's no `slot_disabled` repair;
- the code stays on the lock;
- the switch is untouched where the user left it on;
- the other slot is unaffected.

The rendered repair text is checked through Home Assistant's translation loader. Separate tests cover resuming on a PIN or active change, and when the lock reports the slot empty (keypad delete). The reproduction was first committed as a strict expected failure. Restoring disable-on-clear fails every case.

**Known and left for the refusal-rule refactor:**
- `CodeRejectedError`'s own message still says "cannot set code" where other features show it for a clear: the unmanaged-code repair and the `clear_usercode` action.
- ZHA's lock-specific statuses 2 and 3 get Zigbee's generic status names.

## What R1 is
- **The problem:** "is this slot / lock managed, and by whom" is answered by several predicates that drifted apart. Line numbers below are from main; verify them:
  - `get_managed_slots` (`domain/queries.py`) → `BaseLock.managed_slots` (`providers/_base.py`): every entry, any state, disabled and ignored included. Used for read scope, budgets and confirmation scope.

## Scope discipline
- No behavior change. If you find a caller whose current predicate looks WRONG, don't fix it. Keep today's behavior and list it in the report as a follow-up.

input.message:
The `/code-review` round on R1 confirmed that no caller's behavior changed, and that no removed name is still used anywhere. Fix the following. This is the final round. Same rules as before: commit forward, no push, mutations in scratch only.

1. **AGENTS.md ~80.** The new "Which entry manages this lock or slot" bullet was inserted between the `BaseLock` bullet and its continuation line. "...and `async_call_service()` helper (wraps HA service calls...)" now trails the new bullet. Restore the BaseLock bullet, and put the new bullet after it.
2. **AGENTS.md ~76.** It overstates: "answered only by the named questions in domain/queries.py". Lock-instance questions (`_find_shared_lock_instance`, `_lock_instance_held_by_another_entry`, `iter_loaded_lcm_entries` / `get_managed_locks`) still deliberately filter elsewhere. Say that config questions, meaning which entry's config lists this lock or slot, go through `queries.py`, and that live-instance ownership is separate (R2).
3. **`queries.py` docstring table.** It leaves out the Akuvox and Schlage tag passes (`akuvox.py` ~265, `schlage.py` ~204). These WRITE: they assign untagged device users to `managed_slots - assigned_slots`, which includes disabled entries' numbers. Add them to `slots_configured_on`'s caller list so R1b's per-caller decision sees them.
4. **Pin tests for callers that count disabled entries today.** Decision 5 keeps this behavior, so these stay valid:
   - `websocket._get_slot_entity_ids`: a disabled entry's slot entities still appear in the lock view.
   - `config_flow._check_common_slots`: a new or added lock can't take a disabled entry's slot numbers.
   - `unmanaged.py` sweep: a disabled entry's codes on a shared lock are NOT reported as unmanaged.
   - Each must fail when that site is filtered to enabled-only entries (mutation in scratch).
   - Don't pin the three `another_enabled_entry_configures` sites. R1b changes those.
5. **Differential property test.** Today the property test compares against a re-derived oracle. Make it prove equivalence with the actual old code: put origin/main's bodies of `get_managed_slots`, `find_entry_for_lock_slot` (both modes) and `_lock_managed_by_other_entry` into the test module as frozen references, and assert the new functions equal them over the random entry sets. Keep the existing oracle too if it adds independent value.
6. **Double config build (only if trivial)** (`config_flow.py` ~186, `websocket`). `entries_configuring` throws away the `EntryConfig` it built, so callers rebuild it. Return `(entry, config)` pairs, or skip the build for `excluding`, if that's a small change with no behavior change. Otherwise skip it and say so.

Then run the full suite with coverage (100%) and prek, and report the SHA(s) and the mutant results for item 4.

## Proposed change

"Does an entry manage this lock or slot, and which one?" was answered by several hand-written predicates that had drifted apart. They differed on whether disabled or ignored entries count, which load states count, and whether the first match wins. Each caller picked whichever one it needed.

This is refactor R1 from the coordinator design review. **Behavior does not change.** `domain/queries.py` now exports one named function per question, and its module docstring is the table of which entries each one counts and who asks it:

| Named question | Counts | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `slots_configured_on(lock, *, excluding=None)` | every entry listing the lock, in any state, disabled and ignored included | `get_managed_slots` |
| `configured_owner(lock, slot)` | same set, first match wins | `find_entry_for_lock_slot()` |
| `syncing_owner(lock, slot)` | enabled entries that keep their slots | `find_entry_for_lock_slot(keeping_slots=True)` |
| `another_enabled_entry_configures(entry, lock)` | other entries that aren't disabled or ignored, any state | `__init__._lock_managed_by_other_entry` |
| `entries_configuring(lock)` → `(entry, config)` | the same set as the first row | hand-written scans in `websocket` and `config_flow` |

Every caller moved to the variant it used before. Questions about live lock instances (`_find_shared_lock_instance`, `_lock_instance_held_by_another_entry`) are deliberately left where they are, for the per-lock owner refactor that comes next. AGENTS.md says which questions go through `queries.py`.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [x] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: fixes #
- This PR is related to issue:

**Equivalence.** A property test builds real `MockConfigEntry` sets in random states: enabled, disabled or ignored, any load state, overlapping locks and slots, and stale caches. It asserts that each new function equals main's own old implementation, which is frozen in the test module. It also checks against an independent oracle.

**Tests at the call sites.** New tests pin the behavior of the callers whose choice matters:
- a use of a disabled or failed entry's slot is credited to that entry's user;
- a duplicate code in such a slot is reported as managed;
- a disabled entry's slots still appear in the lock view;
- a new lock can't take a disabled entry's slot numbers;
- a disabled entry's codes aren't reported as unmanaged.

Mutation checks show that each of these tests catches a caller switched to the wrong variant.

**Not changed here:** decision 5 of the review covers which entries should count. R1b will change read scope and the cleanup callers that delete per-lock repairs and stored state.

## 2. The `LockHandle` design

### 2.1 Where it lives
- A new module, `lcm/domain/lock_handle.py`. It imports `async_create_lock_instance` from `domain/locks.py`; nothing in `providers/` imports it.
- The registry is a dict at `hass.data[DOMAIN]["lock_handles"]`, keyed by lock entity id, created on first use. `hass.data[DOMAIN]` is never removed (`__init__.py:598`, `:977`).

### 2.2 Fields
- `lock: BaseLock`.
- `coordinator`: a property returning `lock.coordinator`. Construction stays at `_base.py:895`; moving it is churn that #1629's tests patch around.
- `holders: set[str]`, entry ids.
- `closing: bool`.
- R2b adds `tasks`: a property returning `lock.tasks`.

**Invariant H** (checked by the machine): `entry_id in handle.holders` ⇔ `entry.runtime_data.handles.get(eid) is handle`. Only `acquire`, `release` and `abandon` change either side, synchronously.

### 2.3 `acquire(hass, entry, eid) -> tuple[LockHandle, bool]` (`@callback`, synchronous)
- **Today's pickup rule, preserved in R2a.** Join the registered handle only if some holder other than `entry` is LOADED (the `_find_shared_lock_instance` rule, `__init__.py:1028-1038`).
- **Otherwise build a new handle and register it.** This **supersedes** any registered handle whose holders are all non-LOADED. The superseded handle stays alive with its holders, just as today's second instance does, and closes when they release.
- Both sides of the invariant are updated before returning. The caller then awaits `lock.async_setup_internal(entry)` if the handle was created, or `lock.async_wait_for_setup()` if it joined, exactly as `__init__.py:1842` and `:1858` do now.
- **Why holders must be LOADED today:** so acquisition never joins an instance being torn down (memory `feedback_release_must_invert_acquire`). In the registry, a handle that is closing has already been removed, so that reason disappears. That is Q1 / R2j.
- **FAILED_UNLOAD (accepted gap):** an entry stuck there never releases, so its handle stays alive and keeps the entry as a holder. Under today's rule a new entry supersedes it, giving two instances, as today.

### 2.4 `release(hass, entry, eid) -> LockHandle | None` (`@callback`, synchronous)
- Removes the entry from both sides.
- If the holder set is now empty: sets `closing`, removes the handle from the registry **only if `registry[eid] is handle`**, and returns the handle for the caller to close. Otherwise returns None.
- A missing id or a missing `runtime_data` is a no-op. This keeps `test_async_unload_lock_skips_untracked_lock_entity_id` and `test_releasing_a_lock_from_an_entry_that_never_loaded_purges_every_row` passing.

### 2.5 Closing
- **`async_close(remove_permanently)`:**
  - R2a: `lock.async_unload(remove_permanently)`, then `coordinator.async_shutdown()` if a coordinator exists. Same order as `__init__.py:1108-1115`.
  - R2b: stop `tasks` first.
- **`async_abandon()`:** used for a failed setup. R2a: coordinator shutdown only, matching `:1904-1906`. R2b: also stops `tasks`.
- **`async_unload_lock` keeps its signature;** tests call it directly at `tests/test_init.py:890` and `:2173` and patch it at `:3222`. Its body becomes:
  ```
  closing = {eid: h for eid in ids if (h := release(hass, entry, eid))}   # synchronous
  await _async_stop_slot_sync(runtime_data, ids)                          # unchanged
  for eid, h in closing.items():
      await h.async_close(remove_permanently and not another_enabled_entry_configures(hass, entry, eid))
  ```
- **Failed setup** (`:1896-1906`): `h = release(...)`; if it returns a handle, `await h.async_abandon()`.

### 2.6 `runtime_data.locks` becomes a view
- `domain/models.py:139` becomes `handles: dict[str, LockHandle]` plus a read-only property `locks`, returning a fresh `{eid: h.lock}` dict.
- Every reader in §1.2 keeps working unchanged. The 224 test references read it, and none write it.
- Delete `_find_shared_lock_instance` and `_lock_instance_held_by_another_entry`. Rewrite the docstrings that name them (§1.2).

### 2.7 `spawn` and the task set (R2b)
- **`TaskScope`** goes in a new `lcm/domain/tasks.py` with no dependencies. It is a set of tasks.
  - `spawn(coro, name, *, eager_start=True)` calls `hass.async_create_task`, which keeps HA's shutdown reaping. If the task isn't done, it is added to the set with `add_done_callback(discard)`. After `close()` was called, it closes the coroutine and returns None, to avoid an "never awaited" warning.
  - `async_stop(lock)` closes the scope, waits out the grace, then cancels and gathers what remains.
- **Ownership:** `BaseLock.tasks` is created in `__post_init__` (`_base.py:447`), so borrowed instances and unit-test locks have one too. The handle owns its lifetime: `release` marks it closing, and `async_close` / `async_abandon` stop it. `borrowed_lock_instance` stops it in its `finally`; that is a no-op in practice, since borrowed instances spawn nothing.
- **Grace:** move `SlotSyncManager._grace` (`sync.py:372-397`) into `domain/tasks.py` as a shared function and use it from both places. A task holding the lock's turn gets `STOP_GRACE_SECONDS` measured from when it took the turn (`const.py:253`); any other task is cancelled at once. `tests/test_sync.py`'s grace tests must pass unchanged.
- **Call sites:** `self.spawn(...)` on `BaseLock`; the coordinator calls `self._lock.spawn(...)`. In the review, "handle.spawn" means this lock-level `spawn` backed by the scope the handle stops.
- **`_reconnect_task` is unchanged** in R2b: it keeps its own slot, superseding and immediate cancel. Pinned by `tests/providers/test_base.py`: `test_async_unload_cancels_in_flight_reconnect_task`, `test_handle_state_change_supersedes_prior_reconnect_task`, `test_supersede_drains_prior_reconnect_exception`. Q2 asks about it.
- **The coordinator's tracked `_confirm_task` and its timers** stay as they are.

### 2.8 What replaces `_lcm_config_entry` (R2c)
- **Decision: no owner.** The instance needs no Lock Code Manager entry: config is per holder, and queries already go through R1's named questions.
- R2c removes the argument from `async_setup_internal`, `_async_run_provider_setup`, `_run_provider_setup_bounded` and all 8 `async_setup` overrides.
- The `:1045` guard becomes `_setup_started: bool`, set at the top of `async_setup_internal`. That is the same meaning: "initial setup has begun" (#1321 deferred-setup path).
- `async_create_lock_instance` keeps its entry, but only for the log line.

## 3. Behaviors to preserve

Every test below must pass **unchanged** through R2a and R2b.

| #1478: `test_shared_lock_unloads_when_only_sibling_is_unloaded`, `test_reload_with_unloaded_sibling_does_not_leave_two_instances`, `test_reload_with_loaded_sibling_keeps_sharing_the_instance` | The last holder tears down; a reload rejoins a loaded sibling | Holders are counted by acquire and release; the pickup rule is unchanged |
| #1482: `test_loaded_sibling_without_an_instance_does_not_block_teardown`, `test_lock_leaving_one_entry_is_not_removed_permanently` | Config membership isn't holding; `remove_permanently` is downgraded while another enabled entry lists the lock | Holder set ≠ config; the downgrade stays at the close site |

| #1629: `test_two_entries_unloading_one_shared_lock_at_once_tear_it_down_once` | Pop and check in one step | `release` is synchronous; the view updates immediately |

| #1629: `test_an_entry_unloading_while_another_builds_the_lock_anew_stops_its_own`, `test_a_new_instance_failing_setup_beside_an_unloading_one_is_stopped` | Overlap builds a second instance; each is torn down by its own holders | Supersession in §2.3. **R2j would change both.** |
| #1629: `test_a_poll_in_flight_...`, `test_a_write_failing_...`, `test_a_push_after_...records_nothing` | Records nothing after shutdown | Guards kept; the scheduled poll is HA's own task, not a handle task |
| #1187/#1562: `test_unload_stops_sync_managers_before_callbacks_and_platforms`, `test_unload_cancels_in_flight_sync_tick`, test_sync grace tests | Entry stops its managers first; grace measured from the turn | Order in `async_unload_lock` unchanged; `_grace` moved but its tests are unchanged |
| #1243: `test_unload_preserves_persistent_repair_issues` | Non-permanent unload keeps repairs | Same `remove_permanently` flag |
| #1630/#1632: `test_an_options_save_repairs_an_entry_that_failed_to_load`, `test_releasing_a_lock_from_an_entry_that_never_loaded_purges_every_row`, `test_an_entry_that_failed_to_unload_is_read_from_what_it_stores` | Release with or without `runtime_data`; FAILED_UNLOAD keeps its instance | `release` tolerates a missing `runtime_data`; FAILED_UNLOAD never releases |
| Cancelled setup (`tests/test_init.py` around `:4760-4800`), `test_new_lock_setup_failure_logged_and_lock_excluded` | A cancelled lock setup re-raises; one bad lock doesn't block others | `acquire` happens before the await, as `runtime_data` insertion does today |

**Changes the design would make (each is a question, not done silently):**
- **R2b:**
  - lock-spawned tasks no longer outlive teardown; a spawn after the last release is dropped;
  - an unload can wait up to `STOP_GRACE_SECONDS` for a lock task that holds the turn. Today that task simply keeps running unowned.
  - Both are Q2.
- **R2j:** Q1.
- **R2p:** Decision 2, already approved. Pre-#1629, the creator's preference also suppressed backoff polls; now it never does.

**Old defect seen, queued (class c), not fixed in R2:**
- A failed lock setup leaves the provider's config-entry state listener registered on the dropped instance (`_base.py:887`; the drop at `__init__.py:1904-1906` runs no `async_unload`).
- After R2b, any reconnect that listener spawns is refused once the scope closes, so the remaining leak is an idle listener.
- Calling `async_unload` there is risky: the virtual provider writes its store back on unload (`domain/locks.py:69-73`).

## 4. Test strategy

### 4.1 Property first (R2-0; R2a and R2b strengthen it)
- **File:** `tests/properties/test_lock_handle_machine.py`. A `RuleBasedStateMachine` over 3 entries and locks `LOCK_1`/`LOCK_2`, with each entry's lock list drawn. Runs through the real config-entry harness with MockLCMLock.
- **Rules:**
  - `setup`, `unload`, `reload`, `disable`/`enable` (`async_set_disabled_by`), `remove` (`async_remove`);
  - `options_drop_lock` (`write_entry_config`), `options_add_lock`;
  - `fail_next_setup(lock)`: MockLCMLock claims push but doesn't implement subscribing, which fails setup after the coordinator exists (the #1629 technique);
  - `unload_two_at_once` (`asyncio.gather`);
  - `setup_while_other_unloading`: hold the other entry's `pass_lock`, as #1629's tests do.
  - Each rule ends with `await hass.async_block_till_done()`.
- **Invariants:**
  1. **One live handle.** R2-0 (today's code): no two LOADED entries' views hold different instances for one lock. R2a: at most one registered handle per lock, and any live handle not registered has no LOADED holder. After R2j: at most one live handle per lock.
  2. **Shutdown once, when the holder set empties.** A spy on `LockUsercodeUpdateCoordinator.async_shutdown` (autospec with side effect, as `_watch_coordinator_shutdowns` does) records each coordinator shut down at most once. It is shut down if and only if its instance is held by no entry's view (R2-0) or its handle is closing (R2a).
  3. **No task survives close (R2b).** A closing handle's `lock.tasks` is empty and closed, and none of its tasks is pending in `hass`.
  4. **Holders match views (R2a).** Each handle's holder set equals the entries whose `runtime_data.handles` maps the lock to it.
- **Harness traps** (memory `project_property_based_testing`):
  - one event loop and `async_test_home_assistant` per example, entered with `__aenter__`;
  - teardown runs `hass.async_stop(force=True)` **before** `__aexit__`, or `verify_cleanup` fails on leaked instances;

- **R2a keeps today's pickup rule.** Join the registered handle only if some holder other than `entry` is LOADED (the `_find_shared_lock_instance` rule, `__init__.py:1028-1038`).
- **Otherwise build and register a new handle.** It **supersedes** any registered handle whose holders are all not LOADED. The superseded handle stays alive with its holders, exactly like today's second instance, and closes when they release it.
- **Both sides are updated before returning.** The caller then awaits:

  - `lock.async_wait_for_setup()` if it joined;

- **FAILED_UNLOAD (accepted gap):** an entry in that state never releases, so its handle stays alive with that entry as a holder. Under today's rule a new entry supersedes it, and there are two instances, as today.

- **When it was the last holder:** sets `closing`, removes the handle from the registry **only if `registry[eid] is handle`**, and returns the handle for the caller to close. Otherwise it returns None.
- **No-ops:** a missing id or missing `runtime_data` does nothing. This keeps `test_async_unload_lock_skips_untracked_lock_entity_id` and `test_releasing_a_lock_from_an_entry_that_never_loaded_purges_every_row` passing.

- **R2b:**

- **R2j:** this is Q1.
- **R2p:** Decision 2, approved. Before #1629, the creator's polling preference also suppressed backoff polls; under the new rule it never does.

## 4. Test strategy

### 4.1 Property first (R2-0; R2a and R2b tighten it)
- **The machine:** `tests/properties/test_lock_handle_machine.py`, a `RuleBasedStateMachine` over 3 entries and the locks `LOCK_1` and `LOCK_2`, with each entry's lock list drawn at random. It runs through the real config-entry harness with `MockLCMLock`.
- **Rules:**
  - `setup`, `unload`, `reload`;
  - `disable` / `enable` (`async_set_disabled_by`), `remove` (`async_remove`);
  - `options_drop_lock` (`write_entry_config`), `options_add_lock`;
  - `fail_next_setup(lock)`: the `MockLCMLock` claims push support but doesn't implement subscribing, so setup fails after the coordinator exists (the #1629 technique);
  - `unload_two_at_once` (`asyncio.gather`);
  - `setup_while_other_unloading`: hold the other entry's `pass_lock`, as #1629's tests do.

- **Invariants:**

  2. **Shutdown once, exactly when the holder set empties.** Spy on `LockUsercodeUpdateCoordinator.async_shutdown` (autospec with a side effect, like `_watch_coordinator_shutdowns`). Each coordinator is shut down at most once. It is shut down if and only if no entry's view holds its instance (R2-0), or its handle is closing (R2a).
  3. **No task survives close (R2b).** A closing handle's `lock.tasks` is empty and closed, and none of its tasks is pending in `hass`.
  4. **Holders match views (R2a).** Each handle's holder set equals the set of entries whose `runtime_data.handles` maps the lock to it.
- **Harness traps** (memory `project_property_based_testing`):
  - one loop and one `async_test_home_assistant` per example, entered with `__aenter__`;
  - teardown runs `hass.async_stop(force=True)` **before** `__aexit__`, or `verify_cleanup` fails on leaked instances;
  - set `_min_operation_delay = 0`;
  - don't rely on autouse fixtures (the `INTEGRATIONS_CLASS_MAP` patch, rate limiting, custom integrations, the mock lock and calendar platforms). Move the `mock_lock_config_entry` fixture body (`tests/conftest.py:244-316`) into a plain helper in `tests/common.py` that both the fixture and the machine call;
  - `deadline=None`, a small `stateful_step_count`, and measure how long it runs;
  - before pushing: `rm -rf .hypothesis && HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci ...`. If 200 examples take more than about 60 s, cap the examples for this machine and say so in its docstring.
- **Mutations the machine must catch:**
  - an `await` between `release` removing the entry and checking whether anyone is left;
  - joining a handle that has no LOADED holder (R2a only);
  - `async_close` skipping the coordinator shutdown;
  - the scope's stop skipping the cancel.
- **First commit:** R2-0 is green on the R1 base before any production change.

### 4.2 End to end
- **Unchanged after R2a, R2b and R2b′:** the existing suite, including `tests/test_init.py`, `tests/providers/*/test_e2e.py`, `tests/providers/test_base.py` and `tests/test_sync.py`.
- **One late-answer e2e per site moved to `spawn`.** Each test holds the spawned task at an await, tears down the last holder, then lets the await finish. It asserts the task was cancelled and nothing was recorded: no data, breaker, repair or subscription.
  - `coordinator.py:605`: the breaker trips while its refresh read is held (`tests/test_init.py`).
  - `_base.py:1302`: reachability returns while the refresh is held (`tests/test_init.py`, push-enabled `MockLCMLock`).
  - `_base.py:890`: through the virtual re-setup path (`tests/providers/virtual/test_e2e.py:170`). Note in the PR that only tests reach this path.
  - `_mqtt.py:222`: first a **strict xfail on the R1 base** that confirms the ghost subscription, with the queue order written down. Then on zwave-js-ui and Z2M: unload while `async_subscribe` is pending, and assert no subscription survives and no event fires for the dead instance.
  - R2b′ sites:
    - `matter.py:1562` (LockUserChange, with `_raw_lock_users` held) and `matter.py:1425` (LockOperation), in `tests/providers/matter/test_e2e.py` using the ClearUser harness around `:241`;

    - `zigbee2mqtt.py:256` (`pin_code_added`).
- **Grace:** an e2e where a lock task holds the turn when the handle closes. It finishes inside the grace and is cancelled after it. Use `freezer` with the `_step_clock_until` helpers (memory `reference_ha_test_time_tools`; `tests/providers/test_base.py`, #1628).

## 6. Open questions for Raman

1. **Pickup rule (Q1).** Should acquisition keep joining only a handle with a LOADED holder, or join any registered handle?
   - **Recommendation:** join any registered handle (R2j).
   - **Why:** "LOADED only" exists so that we never join an instance that is being torn down. In the registry that can't happen, because a closing handle is removed in the same synchronous step that finds it has no holders.
   - **What it fixes:** today's rule builds a second live instance for one physical lock whenever an entry sets up while another unloads, and permanently next to a FAILED_UNLOAD holder. That gives two `_aio_lock`s on one lock: the #1562 hazard of interleaved writes, plus duplicate push events.
   - **Cost:** two #1629 tests change. Memory says not to re-flag the rule as drift; this asks only because the registry removes the reason it existed.
2. **Grace on close (Q2).** Should lock tasks get the #1562 grace on close? A task holding the turn would get up to `STOP_GRACE_SECONDS` from when it took the turn, and other tasks would be cancelled at once. Today they keep running with no owner after teardown.
   - **Recommendation:** yes, and give `_reconnect_task` the same rule instead of today's immediate cancel, because Akuvox and Schlage write during it.
   - **How:** a separate, named commit in R2b. It changes the reconnect tests in `tests/providers/test_base.py`.
3. **What "Disable polling" covers (Q3, R2p).** **Recommendation:**
   - it stops only the scheduled poll; the drift hard refresh and the connection checks keep running, as they did before #1629;
   - a lock that hasn't been reached yet counts as a cold-start probe, whether it's a poll or a push provider.

All three answers are recorded in the plan and in memory:
- **Q1:** join any registered lock, so there's one instance per physical lock.
- **Q2:** a bounded grace for lock tasks, including reconnect.
- **Q3:** "Disable polling" stops only the scheduled poll.

**R2-0 is under way** (`refactor/lock-handle-machine`, stacked on R1). It's tests only:
- **The machine:** a stateful property test that drives 2–3 configurations sharing a lock through setup, unload, reload, disable, remove, option changes, failed setups and overlapping unloads. It checks two rules: no two loaded configurations hold different instances of one lock, and each coordinator shuts down exactly once, when nothing holds it.
- **Mutation checks:** it must catch an await between pop and check, and a skipped shutdown on either path.
- **If it finds a real violation in today's code,** that case is recorded as an expected failure rather than fixed in this test-only PR.
- **If cheap:** a reproduction of the suspected MQTT ghost subscription.

**#1634** (R1) is waiting on your review. R2a stacks on it.
how many PRs remain?

About **25 PRs**, counting #1634, which is already open. Some numbers are estimates, as noted.

| Group | PRs | Count |
|---|---|---|
| **Open** | #1634 (R1, "manages" predicates) | 1 |
| **R2: lock ownership** | R2-0 (property machine, in progress), R2a (LockHandle), R2j (join any handle), R2b (base, coordinator and MQTT tasks), R2b′ (provider event tasks), R2c (no configuration in provider setup), R2p (polling rule) | 7 |
| **R1b** | read scope plus the cleanup callers (decision 5) | 1 |
| **R3** | read scope and budget decided once the lock's turn is taken | 1 |
| **R4 + spec C** | refusal rule table; breaker resets on target change | 2 |
| **R5 + spec B** | belief owner in memory; persist it | 2 |
| **R6** | push integrity per provider (zwave-js-ui, Matter, Z2M) | 3 |
| **Gap-fillers** | R7 (Matter duplicate indices), spec D (display sentinels) | 2 |
| **Built-in audit cleanups** | `async_at_started`; test helpers plus faked breaker fields; remaining wall-clock tests onto `freezer`; websocket errors onto Home Assistant's handling | ~4 |
| **The model switch** | E (atomic per the spec; also gives #1622's release clears a judge) | 1, large |
| **#1581** | F (write-only locks, including the ZHA "no such slot" answer and keypad-code protection when adding a lock) | 1+ |

**Total: about 25.** The bulk is small, one-ownership refactors; E and F are the big ones.

Where the count could change:
- **R4 could split.** The refusal table touches every provider.
- **E is the largest by far.** The refactors before it are meant to shrink it, but it may still split during planning.
- **Not counted:** the open `lock_display_name` question, and any new bugs the refactors uncover.

Most of these can run two or three at a time in separate branches. The R2 chain is sequential, and E has to wait for nearly everything before it.
I wonder if we should try rebuilding the integration from scratch. I feel like there's overcomplexities we've adopted through all of our attempts at redesigning

I think the instinct is right, and it fits a pattern you've caught before. Your "this feels overcomplicated" calls have been right each time. And the evidence of the last few days points the same way: most of the eleven design flaws came from earlier redesigns layered on top of each other, not from the lock protocols themselves.

I'd split the question in two, because a rebuild of *everything* and a rebuild of *the core* have very different costs.

**Hard to rebuild, and mostly earned (essential complexity):**
- **Providers:** device knowledge we paid for in bugs. Z-Wave's status-before-code ordering, #819 and #863, ZHA reply matching and quirks, Matter user indices, zwave-js-ui's MQTT and retained replays, Z2M's write-only locks.
- **User-facing surface:** config entries and their migrations through v6, entity IDs, actions, blueprints, the card, repairs. You've said only user-facing things carry a compatibility burden, so a rebuild still has to land on exactly these.
- **Home Assistant lifecycle facts:** the rules #1629, #1630 and #1632 each paid for, such as unload not running at stop, `runtime_data` surviving a failed setup, and a coordinator being tied to its entry.

**Where the accidental complexity lives:** almost entirely in `domain/`. That's the coordinator's pending-write machinery and confirmation look; the sync tick as a second scheduler; beliefs mixed into `data`; breaker plumbing; shared-lock ownership inferred by scanning entries; per-method shutdown flags; several definitions of "manages" and "desired". That's what R1–R5 and E are slowly untangling, roughly 20 PRs, each paying review cost against code we intend to replace.

**So the option I'd seriously consider is a clean-room core rebuild, not a full rewrite:**
- Keep the providers (behind a tightened interface) and the user-facing surface.
- Write a new domain core from the model we've already derived: decisions 1–13, the eleven flaws, and the approved decisions. Its shape is one owner per lock, observations kept apart from beliefs, one judge, and one refusal rule.
- Build it next to the existing core, with property tests as the oracle. Several already exist or are in progress, including R2-0's lifecycle machine. Then switch over and delete the old core.

That could replace most of the remaining refactor queue with one design and one big, well-tested change. The risks are real, though:
- **Big-bang review.** One large change is much harder to review than small ones.
- **Lost bug fixes.** The old core encodes about 40 hard-won fixes that a fresh core could quietly lose. The issue and PR regression review from last week becomes the checklist.
- **Effort split.** Effort goes into the rebuild while bugs keep arriving in the old code.

Before deciding, I'd rather measure than argue. I'd write one short assessment document covering:
1. **How big each module is,** and how much of each is essential versus accidental. Lines spent on each concern, the way your "is the v3 diff too big" question asked.
2. **A clean-room sketch of the core** from first principles: components, ownership, data flow and the provider interface. Plus an estimate of its size compared with today's `domain/`.
3. **Three options compared:**
   - a full rewrite;
   - a core rebuild behind the existing providers and user-facing surface;
   - continuing the refactor queue.

   For each: cost, risk, what we'd lose, and how we'd prove nothing regressed.

Meanwhile I'd pause new refactor work. #1634 (R1) is harmless either way. R2-0's lifecycle property machine is worth finishing, because it would serve as a test oracle for a rebuild too.

Want me to write that assessment?
can we first add tests for all of the bugs that have been reported? then when we switch out the core its lower risk

Yes. That's the right order: a regression net first, then the core swap is checked against it, not against our memory of 40 past fixes. One point makes it work: **the tests have to describe behavior, not internals.** A test that pokes `coordinator._pending` or `_slot_breaker` breaks the moment the core is replaced and proves nothing. Each test should go through things that survive the rebuild: entity states, actions, repairs, and the provider fakes that answer like the real libraries.

**Plan:**
1. **Catalog every reported bug.** That means GitHub issues (open and closed) and every `fix:` PR, plus bugs found in review that were never filed (#1622, the refused-clear loop and so on). Last week's regression review covered 129 issues and 77 fix PRs, so that's the starting point, brought up to date. For each bug: the symptom, the trigger, the provider, the PR that fixed it, and the test that guards it today.
2. **Sort each one into three groups:**
   - guarded by a behavior-level test;
   - guarded only through internals, which needs a behavior-level test;
   - not guarded at all.
3. **Write the missing tests in batches by area** (Z-Wave JS, Matter, ZHA, Z2M, zwave-js-ui, config flow, sync and repairs). Each test must fail when the fix is reverted, which is the same proof we've used all week. Bugs that are still open get strict expected-failure tests, like #1622.

Your standing rule is that test-only PRs are for refactoring tests. This effort is the deliberate exception, since you asked for it.

R2-0, the lifecycle property machine, is worth finishing: it's exactly this kind of behavior-level net. Other refactor work stays paused. I'm starting the catalog now and will bring you the numbers before writing tests.

# Bug regression catalog

**Date:** 2026-10-11. **Code and tests:** origin/main @ `964184be`.
**Purpose:** RE-PLAN 2 in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-08-credential-model-roadmap.md`. Every reported bug should have a behavior-level regression test before the domain core (coordinator, sync, pending writes, breaker, lock ownership) is rebuilt. This file lists the bugs, their guards, and the tests still to write.

**Note on #1634.** The brief said #1634 (`refactor/manages-predicates`) was open. It merged at 2026-10-12 01:45 UTC and is in `964184be`, so every citation here already uses its renamed predicates (`domain/queries.py`).

## Method

- **Sources:**
  - all 130 GitHub issues and 1,148 merged PRs. 178 PRs are fix-titled or close an issue; 19 CI/docs/lint-only PRs were skipped;
  - the 2026-10-08 regression review;
  - the review-found bugs in the roadmap ("Notes carried to PR E", the bug-fix queue), `2026-10-11-coordinator-design-review.md` and `2026-10-11-ha-builtin-audit.md`.
- **Finding guards:**
  - Each fix PR's diff was parsed for the tests it added, then matched by name against main. 92 of the 161 PRs examined still have at least one of their own tests on main.
  - Old PRs whose tests were rewritten were matched to successor tests by symbol and scenario grep.
  - Nine area reviewers read the cited tests and the fix diffs. They ran about 600 of the cited tests on the snapshot, and all passed.
  - For the review-found bugs still on main, throwaway probes reproduced the Z-Wave (3), Akuvox ignored-clear and flow (5) cases. They ran in `/tmp` and are not in the repo.
- **Proven?** is `yes` only when the PR body or commits say the test failed before the fix (failing-first, a revert, mutants, or a committed strict xfail). No reverts were run for this catalog.
- **Rows:**
  - One row per distinct user-visible defect. An issue and its fix PRs share a row; a PR that fixed several defects is split.
  - Issues that were feature requests, questions or chores are left out: 37 of the 130.
  - Issues closed as "not a code defect" are listed with Level `N/A` and are not counted.

### Level definitions

- **B: survives a core rewrite.** The test drives and asserts only through HA surfaces or provider fakes.
  - **B(e2e):** a provider e2e harness with a library-level fake.
  - **B(seam):** a real config entry plus `MockLCMLock`, asserting entity states, repairs, services, events, websocket, or the fake's recorded calls. Static checks of shipped files (strings, services, blueprints) are filed here too, since a core swap doesn't touch them.
  - **B(provider):** only the provider's public contract against a library-level fake, for bugs that live in the provider.
  - **B(flow):** a config, options, reauth or subentry flow driven through `hass.config_entries`.
  - **B(ts):** a vitest test asserting public output.
- **I: tied to core internals.** The test asserts on or drives core internals.
  - This includes `coordinator._pending`, `_failed_writes`, breaker fields, `SlotSyncManager` private state, `_cleared_slots`, private coordinator, sync or `_base` calls, hand-built `calculate_in_sync` snapshots, and patches of `domain.*`.

    - `runtime_data.locks` identity checks (lock ownership);

content.text:
The catalog is done (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-11-bug-regression-catalog.md`). #1634 had already merged before the catalog ran, so its citations use the renamed predicates.

**Coverage of the 203 user-visible defects found:**

| Guard | Count | Survives a core swap? |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior-level test | 101 (23 only partly) | yes |
| Only through core internals | **55** | **no**: they break or go blind |
| No test | **47** (33 still open, 14 fixed) | — |

A core swap today would leave **78 fixed bugs** without a working guard, plus 14 fixed bugs with no test at all. The gap is worst in sync, lifecycle and shared locks, which is exactly the code a rebuild replaces: of its 53 bugs, 24 are guarded only through internals and 11 have no test.

**Why so many depend on internals:**
- The test helper `async_trigger_sync_tick` forces private sync state and calls `_async_tick` directly, in 59 places.
- Assertions on `coordinator.data` and `runtime_data.locks` are the same kind of dependence.

About 30 of these 55 tests are cheap to convert to entity-level checks.

**Harness gaps that block behavior-level tests:**
- **Fakes that hold no state:** the Z-Wave JS fake is a stub, so writes change nothing. The Matter user table is static, and the Schlage, Akuvox and Z2M fakes don't track what's on the lock.
- **No fault injection:** `MockLCMLock` can't simulate "acknowledged but not applied", a refusal, or a hang.
- **Config-flow setup:** config-flow tests skip real entry setup, so reauth is never tested starting from a failed entry.

**New findings along the way:**
- **Akuvox re-sends an ignored clear forever:** 30 clears in 30 ticks, with no repair. It's a sibling of the refused-clear loop.
- **#1536 is only partly fixed:** adding a user still waits on the lock read with nothing on screen.
- **#848 may have partly regressed.** This is from reading the driver code, not proven on a device.
- **Some tests pass only because they assert the buggy behavior.** They're listed in the catalog.

**Proposed batches, each a test-only PR:**
- **0:** harness prep (stateful fakes, fault injection in `MockLCMLock`, a public way to drive sync ticks).
- **1:** convert about 30 internals-based tests to entity-level checks.
- **2:** sync and breaker.
- **3:** lifecycle and shared locks.
- **4–7:** provider end-to-end suites (Z-Wave, Matter, Schlage/Akuvox, Z2M/zwave-js-ui).
- **8:** config flows with real setup.
- **9:** entities, logs and websocket.
- **10:** frontend and packaging (outside the swap).
- **11:** strict expected-failure tests for the open bugs. Four can't be written this way: one needs an upstream fix, two are performance issues, and one is invisible from any surface.

**R2-0 (the lifecycle property machine) and its review:** it passes and catches the lifecycle mutations it targets, but as a *rebuild oracle* it has a flaw. It depends on internals that a rebuild would rename: `runtime_data.locks`, `pass_lock`, a patched coordinator method, and options written around the options flow. The review also found harness problems:
- a regression shows up as a timeout instead of a shrunk counterexample;
- a teardown error can abort the whole test session;
- some rules are weaker than they look.

So I'd rework it inside batch 3, against stable surfaces, rather than ship it as is.

All of these live in `tests/common.py`. Their tests are in the new `tests/test_harness.py`.

**Clock helpers (moved from `test_base.py`).** They are now public: `async_step_clock_until`, `async_run_paced`, `async_settle_background`, `async_run_until_quiet`, `unfinished_tasks` and `CLOCK_STEP`. They still fail the test instead of hanging. `test_base.py` changed only in names and imports, and its tests pass.

**Time-driven sync tick.** `async_advance_sync_ticks(hass, freezer, ticks=1, *, settle=True)` jumps the frozen clock by one tick interval plus `CLOCK_STEP`, so each sync manager's timer fires once, then settles. `async_tick_until(hass, freezer, done, *, max_ticks, what)` keeps ticking until `done` is true and fails with `what` in the message if it never is.
```python
await _async_change_pin(hass, "4321")
await async_tick_until(hass, freezer, lambda: hass.states.get(in_sync).state == STATE_ON,
                       max_ticks=3, what="slot 1 in sync")
```
The docstrings in `tests/conftest.py` now point new tests here instead of `async_trigger_sync_tick` (which drives internals). They also say that `async_advance_time` fires timers but moves neither clock. None of the existing call sites were converted.

**Fault knobs on `MockLCMLock`.** Each one is called as `lock.<knob>(operation, slot=None, *, times=None)` and returns a `LockFault`:
- **`ignore`:** the write reports success but the lock keeps its old code.
- **`refuse`:** raises `CodeRejectedError`, for sets and clears.
- **`fail`:** raises `LockOperationFailed` by default; you can pass any error class or instance.
- **`hang`:** holds the call until the fault is cleared.
- **`drop_reply`:** applies the write, then never answers; clearing the fault raises `LockDisconnected`.

Each fault has a hit count, a `times` limit after which it removes itself, `await fault.async_wait_held()` (bounded, works on a frozen clock), `clear()`, and works as a context manager. Faults can also target reads (`"get"`).
```python
with lock.hang("set", 1) as fault:
    await async_advance_sync_ticks(hass, freezer, settle=False)
    await fault.async_wait_held()
```
A conftest hook releases any fault still holding a call when the test body ends. Without it, teardown hung until pytest-timeout errored at 60 s; with it the test passes in 0.2 s. That scenario is now a permanent test.

**Recording.**
- No-op clears are recorded in `service_calls["noop_clear_usercode"]`.
- Provider setup is recorded in `service_calls["setup"]`.
- `MockLCMPushLock` now has `subscribe_calls` and `unsubscribe_calls` counters. The five bool assertions in `test_coordinator.py` became exact counts, and they pass.

**Breaker without backdating.** `async_trip_slot_breaker(hass, freezer, entry, slot)` makes the slot's writes fail and ticks until the in-sync entity shows `suspended`. It returns the fault so the test can clear it. Two demos use it:
- **Slot breaker:** it trips after exactly 3 real failures, a repair issue appears, and changing the PIN recovers.
- **Lock breaker:** reached with `lock.fail(None, error=LockDisconnected)`, then recovers once the fault is cleared.

The existing backdating tests are not converted.

## Proof the tick is real
Mutation runs, each restored afterwards:
- **Ticks still load state but never sync:** the demo fails with "slot 1 in sync not reached after 3 sync ticks". Both breaker demos and both held-write tests fail too.
- **Interval timer never scheduled:** the demo fails at its first assertion (the slot never loads), and the breaker demo fails.
- **Helper moves no time:** 4 tests fail.

A control test changes the PIN, settles, and moves no time; the lock is never written. Separately, each knob, the no-op recording, the setup recording, the push counter and the teardown release were each broken one at a time, and each break failed at least one harness test.

- **Suite:** 2752 passed, 3 skipped, in 42 s with `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci` and the Hypothesis cache cleared.
- **Coverage:** 100%.
- **prek:** every hook passed on all files.

## Things I noticed
- **Writes that disconnect while reads succeed never suspend.** If only writes raise `LockDisconnected`, each successful read resets the lock breaker, so the slot retries every 2 s indefinitely. This matches the known read-probe-versus-failing-write concern. Because of it, I restricted `async_trip_slot_breaker` to `LockOperationFailed`.
- **In-sync slots never show the lock is unreachable.** The lock-breaker demo needed an out-of-sync slot, because in-sync slots skip the tick. This confirms catalog gap S3.
- **Refused clears say "cannot set code".** `CodeRejectedError` uses that message for clears as well; the catalog already lists this.
- **Ignored writes on the push mock still push.** On `MockLCMPushLock`, an ignored set still pushes the new value, the way ZHA pushes on a success status. This is deliberate and documented.
- **`MockLCMLockWithPush` in `test_base.py`** duplicates the new counters. It could be folded into `MockLCMPushLock` in batch 1.
- **Wrong tick interval in a docstring.** It said 5 seconds; it is 2. I fixed it.
- **Possibly overstated memory note.** `reference_ha_test_time_tools` says pytest-timeout won't break a frozen-clock hang, but it did break the teardown hang described above.
- **Small extra edit.** I added a short note on the new helpers to the Testing Notes in `AGENTS.md`.</result>

Fix exactly these 9 findings (line numbers are approximate, from 8700a9ab). For each, ADD or ADJUST a test in tests/test_harness.py that fails before your fix and passes after (verify the fail-before by temporarily reverting your fix — do mutation checks in a scratch rsync copy under /private/tmp/claude-501/ if you prefer, restoring in a finally; never leave a mutant in the worktree).

1. tests/common.py ~871 `MockLCMLock.clear_faults()` only clears faults still in `self.faults`; `_meet_fault` removes a fault whose `times` is exhausted on its hit, so a held hang/drop_reply with times=N is never released by clear_faults. Fix: clear_faults must release every fault this lock installed (including spent ones still holding a call). Keep the docstring promise "releases any call one holds".
2. tests/common.py ~850 the `hang` docstring tells tests to `await fault.entered.wait()` — unbounded, hangs instead of failing. Change the docstring to direct tests to `await fault.async_wait_held()`.
3. tests/common.py ~698 `async_wait_held` checks `entered`, which is set on the first hold and never reset, so after the held call is released (or for a second call on a times=None fault) it passes while nothing is held. Fix: track the number of calls CURRENTLY held (increment on hold, decrement on release/exit); async_wait_held waits (bounded, failing loudly as it does now) until at least one call is currently held. Keep it bounded. If you keep `entered` as a public attribute, make sure nothing documents it as the way to wait.
4. tests/common.py ~884 `_meet_fault` counts a hit and spends `times` on matching calls the fault cannot affect, e.g. `ignore("set", 1, times=1)` consumed by a set that writes the value already held (NO_CHANGE), or an ignore on a clear of an already-empty slot. Fix: an `ignore` fault only matches (counts a hit / spends times) when the operation would actually change the slot. Check how the mock decides NO_CHANGE and reuse that predicate rather than restating it. Other knob kinds (refuse/fail/hang/drop_reply) keep matching every call — the lock would refuse/fail/hang regardless.
5. tests/conftest.py ~76: faults are released in a `pytest_runtest_call` wrapper, which doesn't run when setup fails, so a fault installed by a fixture stays held through teardown and leaks in the module-level `_INSTALLED_FAULTS` into the next test. A harness test for this may be hard; if you can't write a reliable one, explain why in your report and verify manually.

content.text:
A subagent is now fixing those 9 findings in the batch 0 worktree, adding one new commit on top of `8700a9ab`. Each fix comes with a harness test that has to fail without the fix. I'll check the result against the full suite, coverage and `prek`, then run the second and final review round before opening the test-only PR.

Batch 0 also found a new open bug: if a lock's writes fail as "disconnected" while its reads succeed, the slot never suspends. Every successful read resets the lock breaker, so the slot retries every 2 seconds forever. I've added it to the catalog for an expected-failure test in batch 11.

I also corrected the memory note about pytest-timeout. It didn't stop a busy loop on a frozen clock, but it did stop a teardown stuck waiting on a call, so neither outcome is reliable.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Three of the findings share one root: the harness answered "did this ever happen?" when the test needed "is this happening now?" `async_wait_held` asked whether a call was ever held, not whether one is held now. `clear_faults` released only the faults still listed, not every fault that was installed. `ignore` counted calls that could never have been ignored. A regression test built on that kind of check passes without testing anything.
- Finding 6 matters most for the rebuild: jumping the clock 2 s at once fires every timer due in that window together. A test can then see a race that can't happen in production, or miss one that can. Stepping to each timer's due time in turn keeps them in the same order production would.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
should we revert anything we've merged? or I guess when we do the refactor it will take care of itself?

content.text:
I'd revert nothing, with one exception: `#1629` introduced a regression that needs a small fix before 6.0.2 is published. Waiting for the refactor won't cover it, because the refactor is paused.

**Why not revert the rest:**
- **The fixes hold up.** Nothing we've found shows any merged fix to be wrong. Reverting them would bring back bugs that users reported.
- **The provider fixes are permanent anyway.** `#1624`, `#1625` and `#1627` sit in the provider layer, which a core rebuild keeps.
- **The core fixes pass their behavior to the new code.** `#1623`, `#1629`, `#1632` and `#1633` live in the code a rebuild would replace. Batch 1 turns their tests into checks on entity state that fail when the fix is removed. So what they fixed becomes the spec the new core has to meet, and their code goes away with the old core. That part does take care of itself.
- **`#1634` is behavior-neutral.** The rebuild either reuses its predicate names or deletes them, and reverting now would just be churn.

**The exception:** since `#1629`, the shared lock coordinator has no config entry. As a result, a user's "Disable polling" setting is now ignored for every lock. I logged this in the regression catalog as OPEN, to be fixed in R2. R2 is now paused behind the regression net, though, and 6.0.2 is a draft that already includes `#1629`. Publishing it as-is would ship the regression.

You already approved the rule: poll unless every entry using the lock has disabled polling (decision 2). It's a small fix on its own:
- Override the coordinator's refresh scheduling to check the entries that hold the lock.
- Add one test that drives entity state and fails when the fix is removed.

That doesn't need any of R2's lock-handle work. I'd make it a one-defect PR from main now, in parallel with the batch 0 fixes, and publish 6.0.2 once it merges.

One open question: the R2-0 review found that a failed setup leaves a state listener running. I don't know whether `#1629` caused that or it was already there. Batch 3 will check it with a test, and if `#1629` caused it, it gets the same kind of quick fix.

Should I start the polling fix?
yes

class LockUsercodeUpdateCoordinator(
    DataUpdateCoordinator[dict[CredentialAddress, SlotCredential]]
):
    """Class to manage usercode updates."""

    def __init__(self, hass: HomeAssistant, lock: BaseLock) -> None:
        """Initialize the usercode update coordinator."""
        self._lock = lock
        self._drift_unsub: Callable[[], None] | None = None
        self._connection_unsub: Callable[[], None] | None = None
        # Disable periodic polling when push updates are supported.
        # Polling is still used for initial load.
        #
        # A bridged provider may not know the answer yet: it derives push
        # support from discovery data that arrives on the broker's schedule,
        # so a lock constructed before that lands looks like a poll lock.
        # ``note_push_capability`` is the one place that answer is revisited.
        self._is_push = lock.supports_push
        update_interval = None if self._is_push else lock.usercode_scan_interval
        super().__init__(
            hass,
            _LOGGER,
            name=f"{DOMAIN} {lock.lock.entity_id}",
            update_method=self.async_get_usercodes,
            update_interval=update_interval,
            # Belongs to the lock, which several entries can share, not to any
            # one of them: Lock Code Manager shuts it down once the last entry
            # holding the lock lets go (``async_unload_lock``). The "Disable
            # polling" system option, which Home Assistant reads from a
            # coordinator's own entry, therefore does not apply.
            config_entry=None,
        )
        self.data: dict[CredentialAddress, SlotCredential] = {}
        # Writes the lock has not yet been seen to hold, by address. This is the
        # whole of "unverified": an address is verified exactly when nothing is
        # pending against it. Confirmed by a read or push showing the slot
        # present; given up on by the first read past the deadline that still
        # does not -- which is also the only way a pending write ends without
        # confirmation, so nothing outside a completed read ever has to guess.
        # Keyed by CredentialAddress, NOT by device slot: one slot can hold a
        # credential of each type, and a slot-keyed map would let two addresses
        # sharing a slot consume each other's entry.
        self._pending: dict[CredentialAddress, PendingWrite] = {}
        # Addresses whose pending write failed -- not seen by the deadline, or
        # displaced by a different code -- awaiting the sync tick's one charge
        # to the slot breaker. Consumed by ``take_failed_write``.
        self._failed_writes: set[CredentialAddress] = set()
        # The single confirmation look for this lock: a task for the immediate
        # first look, then a timer while anything stays pending. One per
        # coordinator, not per write: N pending slots on one lock are one read
        # apart, not N.
        self._confirm_task: asyncio.Task[None] | None = None
        self._confirm_unsub: Callable[[], None] | None = None
        self._lock_breaker = CircuitBreaker(
            BACKOFF_FAILURE_THRESHOLD,
            backoff_initial=timedelta(seconds=BACKOFF_INITIAL_SECONDS),
            backoff_max=timedelta(seconds=BACKOFF_MAX_SECONDS),
        )
        self._original_update_interval: timedelta | None = update_interval
        # Whether the lock has ever been reached successfully. A lock that has
        # never been reached is "not ready yet" (e.g. its integration is still
        # starting up after a Home Assistant restart), not "offline" -- so it
        # must not raise the lock_offline repair during the startup window.
        self._reached_once = False

        # Set up drift detection timer for locks with hard_refresh_interval
        if lock.hard_refresh_interval:
            self._drift_unsub = async_track_time_interval(
                hass,
                self._async_drift_check,
                lock.hard_refresh_interval,
                cancel_on_shutdown=True,
            )

        if lock.connection_check_interval:
            self._connection_unsub = async_track_time_interval(
                hass,
                self._async_connection_check,
                lock.connection_check_interval,
                cancel_on_shutdown=True,
            )

    hass: HomeAssistant,
    config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
    lock_entity_id: str,

- Poll unless EVERY entry holding the lock instance has `pref_disable_polling` set. If any holder allows polling, poll. With no holders, poll (the default).

content.text:
Review round 1 on the polling fix found one real defect, and it was reproduced. Polling only restarts when something happens to ask for a refresh.

Here's the failing case. Entry A has polling disabled and holds a lock. Entry B allows polling, has no users, and joins that same lock. Nothing asks for a refresh, so the lock goes without a poll across three scan intervals, even though B allows it.

It currently works for an entry with users only by accident: that entry's slot entities ask for a refresh as they're added. The same gap hits a user-less entry that reloads after polling is turned back on in its settings.

The subagent is fixing it in a new commit:
- **Re-check on join:** when an entry joins a lock it now shares, it schedules a poll if polling is allowed and none is already scheduled. Rescheduling one that's already pending would push it back a full interval.
- **Test for the gap:** a joining entry with no users, which fails without the fix.
- **Test for the real toggle flow:** both entries disable polling, then one turns it back on and reloads, as Home Assistant's settings page does. Polling resumes.
