That breaks "fires once" / "each failure on a tick of its own" and makes async_tick_until counts and async_trip_slot_breaker's MAX_SYNC_ATTEMPTS budget wrong.
   Required invariant: each call fires every sync manager's interval tick EXACTLY once, whatever the starting phase, while still firing other timers in due-time order. Suggested mechanism (your call if you find better): bound the stepping by the sync tick timers' own due times — identify the scheduled sync interval handles, and step through timers in order up to the LATEST of those due times (plus the microsecond landing margin) instead of to start + TICK_INTERVAL + CLOCK_STEP. Since all sync ticks are due within one interval of now, each fires once and its re-arm lands past the bound. Fail loudly if no sync tick timer is scheduled (instead of silently advancing). Make sure the existing "the scheduled tick really runs" tests and the +0.5 s timer-ordering test still pass.
   Add a harness test that pins exactly-one-tick-per-call: count firings of the sync interval tick across calls started at awkward phases (overdue, due within CLOCK_STEP, due exactly at end, freezer.tick(1.996), freezer.tick(1.9995)) and across many consecutive calls (enough to cross the old drift point cheaply — e.g. simulate the drift with freezer ticks rather than 666 calls). cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/pr-polling-body.md <<'EOF'
## Proposed change

Since #1629, every lock's coordinator is built with `config_entry=None`, because one lock's coordinator is shared by every Lock Code Manager entry that holds that lock. Home Assistant applies the "Disable polling" system option inside `DataUpdateCoordinator._schedule_refresh`, by reading the coordinator's own config entry. With no entry, the option was ignored for every lock: a lock kept being polled every scan interval even after the user disabled polling.

This restores the option for shared locks with one rule: **a lock is polled unless every entry holding it disables polling.** If any holder allows polling, the lock is polled. A lock no entry holds is polled too. As with Home Assistant's own option, only the scheduled poll stops. Drift checks, connection checks, the first read, push updates and confirmation reads keep running.

- **`domain/queries.py`:** new `entries_holding`, every entry holding one lock instance in any state, matched by identity. `_lock_instance_held_by_another_entry` (release) now uses it, so "holds" has one definition. It covers the same entries as before.
- **`domain/coordinator.py`:** `_schedule_refresh` reads the holders each time it schedules. `note_holder_joined` re-checks the rule when another entry takes the instance. Without it, nothing would restart polling when an entry that allows it joins a lock every other holder had stopped polling. It schedules only if the rule allows a poll, none is already scheduled, and something listens. That matches Home Assistant, and a join never pushes a due poll a full interval later.
- **`__init__.py`:** the join branch of lock setup calls `note_holder_joined`.

Tests go through real setup with `MockConfigEntry`, the `freezer` fixture and `MockLCMLock` read counts:
- polling disabled stops the scheduled poll;
- the drift check keeps running;
- a shared lock in each combination (one holder disables, both disable, the joiner has no users);
- Home Assistant's toggle flow: `async_update_entry`, then reload, resumes polling;
- a join leaves an already-scheduled poll where it is;
- a lock nothing listens to isn't polled;
- an instance no entry holds is polled.

Every test that checks polling stops fails when the fix is reverted. The tests that check polling continues catch a rule that is too strict (`any` instead of `all`, or checking only one holder), and mutation confirms that.

**Accepted edge cases:**
- **Join during an in-flight poll:** an entry joining while a scheduled poll is running can leave one extra poll behind, if that poll's own reschedule is then skipped (Home Assistant stopping, or listeners removed at the same moment).
- **Entry stuck in FAILED_UNLOAD:** turning polling back on for that entry doesn't restart polling until something else reschedules. Home Assistant only reloads loaded entries on a preference change, and an entry stuck in FAILED_UNLOAD already holds its instance by design.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [x] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: fixes a regression from #1629, unreleased (draft 6.0.2)
- This PR is related to issue: #1629

content.text:
I've opened the polling fix as **#1635** and linked it to this thread. It's ready for your review, and 6.0.2 can ship once it merges.

**The bug:** since #1629, a lock that several entries share has ignored the "Disable polling" setting. That change hasn't been released yet; it's in the draft 6.0.2.

**The fix** follows your rule: a lock is polled unless every entry holding it disables polling.
- It covers only the regular scheduled poll. Drift checks, connection checks, the first read and push updates keep running.
- When another entry starts sharing a lock, the rule is checked again, so a newly added entry that allows polling turns it back on.

**Testing:**
- The full suite passes with 100% coverage, and `prek` is clean.
- Every test that checks polling stops also fails with the fix removed.
- Review hit the two-round cap. Round 1 found the real gap: polling never restarted when a new entry that allows it started sharing the lock. Round 2 found three small issues, two of which were fixed by deleting code.

The PR body names two rare edge cases we're accepting rather than fixing:
- An entry that starts sharing a lock while a poll is running can leave one extra poll behind.
- Turning polling back on for an entry stuck in "failed to unload" doesn't restart polling.

I also marked the regression in the catalog as fixed by #1635.

**Batch 0 harness:** the round-2 fixes are still running: one sync tick per call, faults released in the order they were set, the off-by-one, and cleanup that never touches a closed event loop. Once they come back and check out, I'll open the test-only PR the same way.

Item 5 is only partly provable: the end-to-end test catches the release being moved after teardown, but nothing can catch `tryfirst` being removed, because it makes no difference here.

I checked each item by putting the old code back in a scratch copy under `/private/tmp/claude-501/`, one at a time, restored in a `finally` and since deleted.

**1. Double tick.**
- **Change:** `async_advance_sync_ticks` now finds the scheduled sync interval timers (a Home Assistant interval tracker whose action belongs to a `SlotSyncManager`). It steps through every timer in due order up to the latest of their due times, or up to now if they are overdue. A tick that fires early re-arms 2 s later, which is past where the step stops, so each manager ticks exactly once per call. Other timers on the way still fire in order. It now fails with "no sync tick scheduled" when no entry is loaded.
- **Test:** `test_each_advance_runs_every_sync_tick_exactly_once`. It counts interval firings per manager by recording `_async_tick` calls that get a timestamp; the first tick a manager runs at start gets none and isn't counted. It checks one aligning call, then a phase move, then 6 back-to-back calls. The phases are: overdue, due as the call starts, due within 0.5 ms, due one clock step in, the reviewer's `freezer.tick(1.996)` and `freezer.tick(1.9995)`, and no time between calls.
- **Fail-before:** on 47e0c455's code, 6 of the 7 phases fail with a manager ticking twice, including both of the reviewer's repro phases. "No time between" passes there, which shows the failures come from the phase, not the aligning call.
- **Drift:** a one-off probe (not committed) ran 700 back-to-back calls and every one fired each manager exactly once, which crosses the old call-666 drift point.
- **Existing tests:** the scheduled-tick tests and the +0.5 s timer-ordering test still pass.
- **Tests that now need a loaded entry:** three clock tests. The two-clocks test now asserts both clocks moved the same amount and by more than 2 intervals across 3 calls, not at least 3 intervals. Each call now only moves to the next tick, so a call after the first moves slightly under 2 s.
- **New test:** `test_advancing_sync_ticks_fails_with_no_sync_tick_scheduled`. Reverting the check makes it fail.

**2. Release order.**
- **Change:** `_INSTALLED_FAULTS` is now a dict, which keeps install order. `clear_faults` and `release_all_faults` release in that order.
- **Test:** `test_clear_faults_releases_held_calls_in_install_order` holds 20 writes and checks they answer in install order.
- **Fail-before:** going back to set order fails it, 5 out of 5 runs.

**3. Off-by-one in the 1000-jump cap.**
- **Change:** the stepping is now `_async_step_timers_to`. It always jumps at least once (so an overdue timer fires), and checks whether it has reached the end after each jump, so finishing on the last allowed jump succeeds.
- **Test:** `test_stepping_may_reach_the_end_on_its_last_allowed_jump` sets the cap to 1.
- **Fail-before:** the old check-at-the-top loop fails it.

**4. Release after the loop closes.**
- **Change:** the teardown hook still releases everything before fixture teardown. Afterwards it only calls the new `forget_all_faults()`, which empties the registry without setting any event.
- **Test:** the hook test now has a late fault holding a call while the hook finishes. It asserts the call is still held, and that `clear_faults` no longer sees the fault, then releases it by hand.
- **Fail-before:** putting `release_all_faults()` back in the `finally` fails it.

**5. Proving pytest's ordering.**
- **Release moved after teardown:** `test_a_write_left_held_does_not_hang_teardown` catches this. Its teardown hangs until pytest-timeout (60 s) errors it, so it is caught as a hang, not as a quick failure.
- **`tryfirst` removed:** no test fails, and none can. `tryfirst` only orders wrapper hooks among each other; any wrapper's code before its `yield` already runs before the built-in teardown that runs the fixture finalizers. Nothing else in this suite wraps `pytest_runtest_teardown`, so `tryfirst` makes no difference today. It only guards against a future wrapper. I kept the hand-driven hook test and its docstring points to the end-to-end test.

**Verification:**
- **Full suite:** `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci pytest tests/ -n auto --cov` gives 2773 passed, 3 skipped. `custom_components` is at 100%. The uncovered lines in `tests/common.py` were already uncovered before.
- **Harness:** `tests/test_harness.py` passed 53/53 on each of 3 runs.
- **prek:** passes.
- **Pyright:** no new diagnostics in the three files.

**Open risk (not fixed, to keep this narrow):** the settle after each call steps up to about 0.6 s. If sync managers have different phases (for example, one restarted after a reload) and settling takes longer than the gap between their due times, the earliest manager's next tick could fire inside the settle. With test operation delays at 0, settling normally takes a few milliseconds, and no current test hits this.</result>

## Proposed change

This is batch 0 of a regression-test net. Every reported bug should get a test through Lock Code Manager's user-facing surfaces (entity states, actions, repairs, flows, events) before the domain core is reworked. This PR only builds the harness those tests need. It adds no bug tests and changes no production code.

**Clock helpers** for Home Assistant's `freezer` fixture, which moves both `time.monotonic` and the event loop's clock. The helpers are shared in `tests/common.py`, moved out of `tests/providers/test_base.py` (#1628):
- `async_step_clock_until`
- `async_run_paced`
- `async_settle_background`
- `async_run_until_quiet`

**Time-driven sync tick:**
- **`async_advance_sync_ticks`** runs the real scheduled sync tick by moving the clock. It doesn't call sync internals. It steps through timers in the order they come due, so a confirmation read due 0.5 s into the window runs before the tick, as it would in production. Each call fires every sync manager's tick exactly once, whatever phase the tick starts at. It fails loudly when no sync tick is scheduled or too many timers come due.
- **`async_tick_until`** steps ticks until a condition on the user-facing state holds, with a bound, and fails with a named description otherwise.
- **`async_trip_slot_breaker`** suspends a slot through real failed writes. It only rewrites "never suspended" failures; a failure to settle comes through unchanged.

**Fault knobs on `MockLCMLock`** (`ignore`, `refuse`, `fail`, `hang`, `drop_reply`). Each takes an operation, an optional slot and an optional `times`, and returns a `LockFault` with:
- a hit count;
- `held` (calls held right now);
- a bounded `async_wait_held()`;
- `clear()`;
- context-manager use.

How the knobs behave:
- **Ignore:** an `ignore` only counts writes that would change the slot.
- **Held reads:** a held read reports which slots it covers when it answers, as a real provider walking its slots would.
- **`run_times`:** records a call only once it reaches the lock.
- **Release:** `clear_faults` releases held calls in install order.
- **Teardown:** a `pytest_runtest_teardown` wrapper releases every held call before fixture teardown, so a held write can't hang the test's teardown. Leftovers are then only forgotten, never released, because by then the event loop may be closed.

**Recording:** no-op clears, setup calls, and push subscribe/unsubscribe counts on `MockLCMPushLock`.

**Defaults:** `MockLCMLock`'s default behavior is unchanged for tests that install no faults. `tests/test_coordinator.py` only swaps three boolean flags for counts.

`tests/test_harness.py` tests the helpers themselves, 53 tests in about 3 s. Mutation checks confirm that suppressing the scheduled sync tick fails the time-driven tests, so the helper really runs the tick. Each review finding has a test that failed before its fix.

**Known limit:** after each call, `async_advance_sync_ticks` settles background work by stepping the clock for up to about 0.6 s. If two sync managers' ticks were further apart in phase than that settle (for example, one restarted after a reload) and settling took longer than the gap, the earlier manager could tick again inside the settle. Test operations take no time, so settling takes milliseconds and no current test hits this.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [x] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue:
- This PR is related to issue: #1628 (helpers moved from there)

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

Both PRs are open, linked to this thread, and ready for your review:

- **#1635:** the fix for "Disable polling" being ignored on locks shared by several entries. This came from #1629. It should merge before 6.0.2 is published.
- **#1636:** batch 0 of the regression net. It's the test harness only; there's no production code in it.

**About #1636:**
- **What it adds:**
  - a sync-tick helper that moves the clock to run the real scheduled tick;
  - helpers that run ticks until a condition holds, or until a slot's breaker trips;
  - five fault knobs on the mock lock (ignore, refuse, fail, hang, drop reply);
  - teardown that can't hang on a held call.
- **Results:** the full suite passes (2773 tests) with 100% coverage, and `prek` is clean. The harness's own 53 tests run in about 3 s, and each review fix has a test that failed before it.
- **Reviews:** it took the two allowed rounds. Round 2 caught a bug my round-1 fix had introduced: one helper call could fire a sync tick twice. The fix and a test pinning "exactly one tick per call" are in.
- **Known limit, written up in the PR body:** if two sync managers tick at very different times, one could tick again while background work is settling. No current test runs into this.

Once #1636 merges, batch 1 starts. It converts about 14 bugs whose tests check internals into tests on what users see: entity states, actions and repairs.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The harness PR changed shape across the two review rounds, but every finding was in test code that the branch itself had introduced. That's the case where fixing in place is right. Backing out applies when fixes start touching the design itself.
- One finding couldn't be pinned down: `tryfirst` on the teardown hook. pytest runs any wrapper's code before its `yield` ahead of the built-in fixture teardown anyway, so `tryfirst` only matters once a second wrapper exists. When a mutation survives, check whether the guard has any effect today before writing a test for it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
Both merged

A rebuild breaks or blinds those.

- Drive ONLY through Home Assistant surfaces or the library-level fakes: real config entries set up via hass.config_entries, entity states (in-sync binary sensor, code sensors, active/enabled entities), repairs (issue registry, e.g. `slot_suspended`), events, services/actions, the provider e2e harnesses' fake nodes/clients and their recorded calls, `MockLCMLock`'s recorded `service_calls`.

Batch 1 has started. With #1635 merged, the polling regression is fixed on main, so the 6.0.2 draft can be published whenever you're ready.

**Housekeeping:**
- Removed the three worktrees whose branches have merged (`shared-lock-polling`, `regression-harness`, `manages-predicates`) and deleted their local branches. Before removing them I checked each one: the only uncommitted change was the tool-written `.entire/.gitignore` line.
- Kept `refactor/lock-handle-machine`. It gets reworked in batch 3.
- In the catalog, I took "Disable polling" off the open-bug list. #1635's tests now guard it.

**Batch 1** (`test/regression-batch1`, worktree `.worktrees/regression-batch1`) is underway. A subagent is adding a user-facing test next to each of 13 bugs that are currently guarded only by tests on internals:
- **Z-Wave JS:** #819/#1625, #863, #1327, #1321, #776.
- **Z-Wave JS UI:** #1471's stale Available, #1624.
- **Shared locks:** #1623, #1629.
- **Startup and sync:** #358, #101, #737's drift path, #1437.

The ground rules for each new test:
- **What it may touch:** it uses only real setup, entity states, repairs and the fake device's recorded calls.
- **How time moves:** only through batch 0's time-driven tick.
- **Must fail without the fix:** each test has to fail when its fix is reverted, checked in a scratch copy.
- **Old tests stay:** the existing internal tests remain until the core is swapped.
- **Bugs aren't fixed here:** if it finds a real bug, it stops on that item and reports it.

One case is deliberately left out: the masked variant of #863. Today's test pins the behavior of an open bug ("#863 vs #819"), so converting it would encode the bug as correct. It goes to batch 11 as a strict expected-failure test.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- "Must fail with the fix reverted" is the test of whether a guard is real. A new test that passes either way is just describing the code.
- Keeping the internal tests alongside the new ones is deliberate. For now both sets agree. When the core is swapped, the internal ones break, and the user-facing ones are what tell us the new core still behaves.

Batch 1 is back with the subagent to fix what the first review round found. It hasn't been pushed, and this is round 1 of the two-round limit.

The first draft added a user-facing test for 12 of the 13 bugs, each proven to fail when its fix is removed. The 13th, #358, has no fix left in the code to remove, so the #101 test checks its symptom instead. The review found six problems:

1. **Input the driver never sends (#863, #1623):** these tests send an "Available" status on its own. The reviewer read node-zwave-js and found the driver always reports status and code together. Sent the real paired report, LCM wrote the slot again. The subagent will first check that claim itself against the driver source, tracing through the server and client libraries to HA's Z-Wave JS integration.
   - Then it measures how LCM handles each possible paired code: the leftover PIN, empty, `0000` and `****`.
   - If LCM writes a bounded number of times and then settles, that guards the bug as reported ("rewritten forever").
   - If it loops, that's a real bug, and the subagent will stop and report it rather than fix it.
   - Whether an "Available" paired with an empty code should be trusted is still the open "#863 vs #819" question, so no test will settle it either way.
2. **The fake Z-Wave lock doesn't behave like the driver.** It skips the credential events the driver sends after a successful write. It reports the old code after a clear, where the driver records an empty slot. It raises an error on clearing an empty slot, where the driver succeeds.
3. **#776 turns masking on halfway through the test.** A real masking lock masks from the start. The test will instead check that each masked slot is written at most once and never again.
4. **#101 never reaches the startup window its fix covers.** If no setup driven through real entities can reach it, I'll report #101 as only partly converted.
5. **A harness helper skips tasks by name.** It will skip only the specific Z-Wave JS listen task instead.

The subagent also raised a design question, which I've added to the catalog to bring to you before the core rebuild. If a slot's condition entity doesn't exist yet when sync starts, the slot is treated as inactive. It gets cleared, then set again once the entity appears. That's #101's symptom, but it only happens when the condition's integration loads after Home Assistant finishes starting. Should a missing condition entity mean "not ready yet" instead?

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The main finding is the "tests must not build their own input contract" lesson coming back. A hand-written report the driver can't produce shows that LCM handles a made-up input, not that the bug is guarded. Checking the input against the driver source is part of writing the test.
- The open "#863 vs #819" question shows up again here. Batch 1 can guard what was actually reported (an endless rewrite) without deciding which "Available" reports to trust. That keeps a test-only PR from quietly making a design call.

Batch 1 is open as **#1637** and linked to this thread. It adds no production code.

It adds tests for 13 fixed bugs that were previously guarded only by tests reaching into internals. The new tests work only through real setup, entity states, repairs and the calls the fake device records, and each one fails when its fix is reverted. The old internal tests stay until the core is swapped.

Two bugs are only partly covered:
- **#358** has no fix left in the code to revert. Its symptom, a sensor showing `unavailable` at startup, is checked inside the #101 test.
- **#101**'s "wait for the slot's state to load" can't be reached from Home Assistant's side, so that part is still guarded only at the internal level.

Review used both rounds:
- **Round 1:** some tests were sending Z-Wave reports the driver never produces. The subagent checked five claims about driver behavior against the node-zwave-js source, and all five held. The fake lock now behaves like the driver.
- **Round 2:** narrow fixes only, such as an exact write count for #776, a fake that matches the driver more closely, and one shared set of event builders.

The suite passes (2805 tests, 3 skipped) with 100% coverage, and `prek` is clean.

The PR body lists the three open bugs this batch found, and my earlier question still stands. Should I file these two as GitHub issues?
- **Joining entry's slots stay unavailable.** When a second entry joins a shared push lock, a push in the first ~10 s cancels that entry's first read, so its slots stay unavailable.
- **#863 still loops for some locks.** A lock that reports "Available" with an empty, `0000` or `****` code after every set is rewritten forever. It's the set-side twin of #1622.

A third finding is milder and not confirmed yet. When the lock reports "Available" with a `****` code, LCM reads `****` as the actual code. I'd keep it in the catalog only.

Batch 2 (sync, breaker and repairs, about 20 bugs) can start once you've merged #1637 or told me to stack it on top.

You are writing batch 2 of a regression-test net for the Lock Code Manager Home Assistant custom integration. TEST-ONLY PR: no production code changes (custom_components/ untouched). If you find a real bug, STOP that item and report it with a reproduction; do not fix it.

WORKTREE (absolute paths only; never touch /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager itself or other worktrees): /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/regression-batch2
Branch: test/regression-batch2, STACKED on test/regression-batch1 (PR #1637, unmerged; HEAD 74324157). Commit on top (one or a few commits), do NOT push. Never run bare `git stash`. Read AGENTS.md first (it documents the harness). Create a venv in the worktree if needed (`uv venv --python 3.14 && uv pip install -r requirements_dev.txt`; .venv is gitignored); `yarn install` if prek's eslint needs it.

## Why
The domain core (coordinator, sync tick, pending writes, breakers, lock ownership) may be rebuilt. Every fixed bug needs a guard that survives that. These bugs (sync / breaker / repairs) are guarded today only at the "I" level (tests driving or asserting core internals: `_async_tick`, `_state`, `_min_operation_delay`, `_execute_rate_limited`, `_setup_succeeded`, `_setup_deferred`, breaker fields, hand-built `calculate_in_sync` snapshots, patches of `domain.*`), partially, or not at all.

## Rules for every new test ("B level")
- Drive ONLY through Home Assistant surfaces or library-level fakes: real config entries via hass.config_entries, entity states (in-sync binary sensor, code sensors, active sensor, switch, text), repairs (issue registry: slot_suspended, slot_disabled, lock_offline, lock_setup_failed…), events, services/actions, provider e2e fakes and their recorded calls, `MockLCMLock`'s recorded `service_calls`, `lock.codes`, `run_times`.
- Time moves ONLY via the batch 0 harness in tests/common.py: `async_advance_sync_ticks`, `async_tick_until(..., max_ticks=..., what=...)`, `async_trip_slot_breaker`, the clock helpers (`async_step_clock_until`, `async_run_paced`, `async_settle_background`), and MockLCMLock fault knobs (`ignore/refuse/fail/hang/drop_reply` with `times`, `async_wait_held`). Read tests/test_harness.py for usage. `freezer` must come before any fixture that sets up an entry. Never `async_trigger_sync_tick`.
- Assert NOTHING internal: no coordinator.data, private attributes, or patches of domain.*.
- Tests must not build their own input contract: feed scenarios the way the real lock/library would. For the ZHA e2e harness, check what zigpy/the real lock would actually send before writing a reply. Batch 1's review caught tests sending reports the Z-Wave driver never produces; don't repeat that.
- Prefer exact counts over bounds when the exact count is stable (a `<= 1` let a mutant through in batch 1). Prefer condition-based waits (`async_tick_until`) over fixed tick counts that happen to be the minimum.
- ADD the B test next to the existing I test; do NOT delete or rewrite I tests.
- Each new test MUST FAIL with its fix reverted. Prove it per test in an rsync scratch copy under /private/tmp/claude-501/ (restore in a `finally`; never leave a mutant in the worktree): revert the PR's change (`gh pr diff <n>`, `git log -S`) or the narrowest mutation of the guarding logic. A test that doesn't fail when its fix is reverted is not a guard: keep working on it or report it as not convertible with the reason.
- Never-fixed rows (#199/#209) are non-regression tests of current behavior: if the test fails on main, that's a real bug — stop and report.

## The bugs (catalog rows: bug | scenario | current guard | suggested B guard)
1. #59 / PR #66 — adding a condition to a configured slot leaves the PIN on the lock (config edit adds a condition entity that is off). Current: B partial (active sensor only). B: after the config change (through the real flow/subentry path the user would use, not a direct write if a flow exists), advance ticks; slot absent from `lock.codes`, in-sync `on`.
2. #63 / PR #66 — changing the PIN on an in-sync slot never pushes the new code. I: test_binary_sensor.py::test_pin_change_during_sync_uses_snapshot; ::test_handles_disconnected_lock_on_set. B: zha e2e (or seam): set the PIN text entity to a new value, advance; the lock holds the new PIN, in-sync `on`.
3. #405 item 2 / PR #532 — unpaced, redundant operations; retries against an offline lock. I: tests/providers/test_base.py::test_rate_limiting_mixed_operations; test_binary_sensor.py::test_multiple_slots_sync_sequentially_not_concurrently. B: seam + freezer: 2 out-of-sync slots and an offline lock (MockLCMLock disconnected via a surface/fault knob); one set per slot once online, paced gaps in `run_times`, no writes while offline.

Write a seam test (refuse a write, observe the gap before the next operation in run_times). If unpaced, that's an open bug: report it with the reproduction (don't fix, and don't commit a test asserting the unpaced behavior).
4. #102 / PR #123 — failed set/clear never retried. Current: B partial (zha e2e). Gap: disconnect-then-reconnect retry. B: seam: lock disconnected, change PIN, reconnect, advance; lock.codes has the new PIN.

B: seam: the provider's setup/capability probe fails (fault knob or MockLCMLock setup failure through its public hook); no set_usercode calls, no slot repairs, the lock's entities show it unavailable/suspended as the product exposes; once setup validates, the PIN is written.

17. PR #1527 — wedged availability probe / mutex wait / async_setup still parked things. I. B: seam + freezer: the entry reaches LOADED and the slot leaves syncing despite a hung availability probe / provider setup.

Batch 2's round-1 fixes are underway on `test/regression-batch2`. The two never-failing assertions will count attempts that actually reach the lock, the six waits get headroom, and the fault knob will reject a slot it can't use. Round 2, the last one, follows.

Batch 2 also confirmed new bugs, now in the catalog. I copied their reproduction scripts into the local, gitignored `docs/superpowers/repros/` so they survive temp cleanup.

**Open bugs confirmed:**
1. **The operation after a refused write isn't paced.** With the real 2 s delay, the next set reached the lock 0.0 s after a refusal. This was batch 0's unverified finding, now reproduced.
2. **Stale strikes suspend a slot while a write is pending.** Two failures on an old PIN, then a write that lands but can't be confirmed yet, then the user changes the PIN. A single failure on the new PIN then suspends the slot with "failed after 3 consecutive attempts". It's the same family as #1050, on a path that fix didn't cover.

**Design question for the rebuild:** a write that hangs every time is cut off and retried every 10 minutes, forever. The slot shows "syncing" and no repair ever appears, because successful reads in between keep resetting the lock breaker.

That's the same root as batch 0's "writes disconnect while reads succeed" finding, and the opposite of what #1525 intended. Successful reads clearing the record of failed writes now shows up in three findings. That makes it a strong candidate for the refusal rule (flaw 9) and the judge (decision 6).

**Rebuild input:**
- Three breaker resets overlap; any one of them alone fixes #1050.
- Two `int()` casts became dead once storage started converting the slot keys.
- #987(c) can't be tested through Home Assistant's interface, so it stays at the internals level.

Still waiting on you: should I file GitHub issues for the open bugs? Batches 1 and 2 have now found five:
- a joining entry's slots stay unavailable;
- #863 still loops for some locks;
- the operation after a refused write isn't paced;
- stale strikes suspend a slot while a write is pending;
- writes that hang every time churn forever with no repair.

Batch 2's final fixes are running. They're all test-side:

- **#405 counts operation attempts only.** It will no longer count every availability check, so a harmless change to the reachability check can't break it.

- Each changed wait now has room to spare. The tightest is 95 of 243 ticks.

When it finishes, I'll open batch 2 as a test-only PR stacked on #1637, with its base set to `test/regression-batch1` so the diff shows only batch 2.

I haven't filed GitHub issues for the five open bugs from batches 1 and 2; that still needs your yes.

content.text:
Batch 2 is open as **#1638** against `main`, linked to this thread. It's test-only and covers 19 sync, breaker and repair bugs.

You merged #1637 while batch 2 was in review, so I rebased batch 2 onto main before opening it. The squash merge matched batch 1 exactly, and the rebased tree is identical to the commit that passed review. Nothing changed in the move. I also removed batch 1's worktree and branch.

**What's in it:** each of the 19 tests fails when its fix is reverted. That was checked again after both review rounds.
- **Round 1:** two assertions could never fail, and six waits were sized exactly at the minimum.
- **Round 2:** the #405 count of 5 relied on an implementation detail. It now counts only attempts by actual operations.
- **Results:** the full suite passes (2844 tests) with 100% coverage, and `prek` is clean.

**One coupling to look at:** the #405 test has to tell an operation's availability check apart from the 30 s connection check. The mock lock does that by checking the caller's function name, `async_internal_is_reachable`. That ties one harness record to a core method name, which this net is meant to avoid.
- If the rebuild renames that method, the test fails loudly rather than passing blind.
- I couldn't find a way to tell the two checks apart from outside the core, so I left it and named it in the PR body.
- I'd revisit it during the rebuild.

**Not converted:** #987(c) can't be reached through any Home Assistant surface, so it stays guarded only by its internals test.

**Still waiting on you:** should I file GitHub issues for the five open bugs?
- a joining entry's slots stay unavailable;
- #863 still loops for some locks;
- the operation after a refused write isn't paced;
- stale strikes suspend a slot while a write is pending;
- writes that hang every time churn forever with no repair.

Next is batch 3, lifecycle and shared locks. Should it start on top of #1638 or wait for the merge? Batch 3 also includes reworking the lock-handle machine (`refactor/lock-handle-machine`).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Checking that the tree is identical (`HEAD^{tree}`) is a cheap way to prove a rebase changed nothing. Two commits with the same tree hash have byte-identical content, so the review and test results carry over without a rerun.
- The `attempt_times` coupling shows a limit of testing only through surfaces. Some symptoms, like "retries hammer an offline lock", never reach the lock, so nothing outside the core records them. Rather than hide that, the PR names it so it can be revisited in the rebuild.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

merged 1638. Sure create bugs. Kinda crazy that we have all of these bug fixes in this release yet we want to call it a minor. I suppose it's because we're handling a bunch of edge cases? We may want to consider updating PR titles to make that clear so that the release notes aren't alarming. Just a thought

### What happened?

When a user is deleted, Lock Code Manager releases their slot and clears the code on the lock (`async_release_managed_slot`). If the lock acknowledges that clear without applying it, the deleted user's PIN keeps opening the door. Nothing reports it or retries.

Examples of a lock that does this:
- a ZHA lock that answers with a success Default Response but drops the command;
- a Z-Wave lock behind zwave-js-ui that receives an unsupervised User Code Set and ignores it.

Today Lock Code Manager reports the slot as empty after any clear that returns, so the problem is invisible:
- the slot has already left the configuration, so no sync manager re-checks it;
- the unmanaged-code sweep runs only at migration;
- no repair is raised.

This is the same outcome as #1453 (deleted users kept working), reached through a different path: there the clear was never sent, here it is sent and silently ignored.

Expected: a release clear that the lock does not confirm is read back. If the code is still there, Lock Code Manager retries, or at least raises a repair telling the user the deleted user's code may still open the door.

Found while reviewing #1621 (closed). Doing the read-back properly depends on the coordinator refactor planned after the current bug-fix PRs, so this is tracked here until then.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Use a lock that acknowledges a PIN clear without applying it: a ZHA lock replying with a success Default Response, or an unsupervised User Code Set through zwave-js-ui.
2. Create a Lock Code Manager user with a PIN and let it sync to the lock.
3. Make the lock ignore the next clear (on real hardware: a weak mesh link, or a lock that drops the command).
4. Delete the user in Lock Code Manager.
5. The slot shows as empty in Lock Code Manager, but the PIN still unlocks the door, and no repair is raised.

### Home Assistant Version

2026.9.0

### What version of Lock Code Manager are you running?

6.0.1

### Lock make and model

Any lock whose clear can be acknowledged without being applied (seen in code review for ZHA and zwave-js-ui; not yet reproduced on hardware).

### Anything else?

### What happened?

When a second Lock Code Manager entry starts using a lock that another entry already manages, the new entry's slots have no data until the lock's coordinator does a delayed (debounced) read, about 10 s later. If the lock pushes any update during that window (a keypad use, a code report for another slot, the first entry's own writes landing), Home Assistant's `DataUpdateCoordinator.async_set_updated_data` cancels the pending debounced read. A push lock never polls, so nothing schedules another read, and the new entry's slot entities (in-sync, code sensor) stay unavailable until something happens to report those exact slots.

Expected: the new entry's slots are read and show their state within a few ticks, whether or not the lock pushes in the meantime.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Set up entry A with a Z-Wave JS lock (a push lock) and a user on slot 1.
2. Set up entry B on the same lock with a user on slot 3.
3. Within ~10 s of entry B's setup, have the lock report anything for slot 1 (for example a keypad code change).
4. Entry B's slot 3 in-sync and code sensors stay unavailable (30 sync ticks in the reproduction). Without step 3, slot 3 is in sync by about the third tick.

Reproduced in the test harness (Z-Wave JS end-to-end setup); found while writing the regression tests in #1637. A slot added to an existing entry while a push lands probably hits the same path (not tested).

### Home Assistant Version

2026.9.4

main after 6.0.1

### Lock make and model

Any push lock shared by two Lock Code Manager entries (reproduced with Z-Wave JS).

Related: #1629, #1635 (shared lock coordinator).

cat > 2.md <<'EOF'
### What happened?

#863 stopped Lock Code Manager from rewriting a wanted PIN forever when the lock sends a stale "Available" status shortly after a set. It only holds when the report's code field still contains the PIN. node-zwave-js always writes `userIdStatus` and `userCode` together, and emits a value event even when a value is unchanged. So a lock that re-announces "Available" after every set produces a paired report with whatever code the lock sends.

Measured in the test harness for a lock that reports Available about 3 s after every set, over 20 sync ticks:

| Code paired with Available | Rewrites |
|---|---|
| the PIN just written | 0 |
| `""` | 10 (one per set, forever) |
| `0000` | 10 |
| `****` | 10 |

The slot is never suspended and no repair is raised, because each set call succeeds. This is the set-side twin of #1622: the lock acknowledges a write that does not stick, and the failure is never counted.

Expected: a slot that keeps being written and keeps reading back as not holding its PIN is eventually suspended with a repair, instead of looping forever. Whether "Available" with an empty code right after a set is a stale report or a real deletion is a separate design question; the loop is a bug either way.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Use a Z-Wave lock that reports `userIdStatus` Available a few seconds after each successful User Code Set, with an empty, `0000` or `****` code.
2. Give a Lock Code Manager user a PIN on that lock.
3. Watch the lock's commands: the PIN is written again after every Available report, indefinitely.

### Home Assistant Version

2026.9.4

### What version of Lock Code Manager are you running?

main after 6.0.1

### Lock make and model

Any Z-Wave lock that re-announces Available after a set (reproduced in the test harness; the pairing behavior was verified in the node-zwave-js source, `UserCodeCC.ts` `persistUserCode` and `ValueDB.setValue`).

### Anything else?

Related: #863, #1622, #1637.

cat > 3.md <<'EOF'
### What happened?

Lock Code Manager spaces operations on a lock by its minimum operation delay (2 s by default), but it only records the time of an operation when the call succeeds (`BaseLock._execute_locked` updates `_last_operation_time` after the call returns). A write the lock refuses is still a round trip to the device, yet the next operation goes out immediately.

Measured with the real 2 s delay and a lock that refuses one set: gaps between operations reaching the lock were 2.0 s, 0.0 s, 2.0 s, 2.0 s. A lock that keeps refusing gets its next command with no spacing each time.

Expected: every operation that reaches the lock, refused or not, counts toward pacing.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Set up a lock with two slots out of sync.
2. Make the lock refuse the first slot's set (for example a Supervision Fail, or a Zigbee lock rejecting the code).
3. The second slot's set reaches the lock immediately after the refusal, with no 2 s gap.

Reproduced in the test harness while writing the regression tests in #1638.

### Home Assistant Version

2026.9.4

main after 6.0.1

Any (provider-independent; in `BaseLock`).

### What happened?

#1050 fixed stale failure strikes from an old PIN suspending a slot on the next PIN change. The same thing still happens when the change arrives while a write is waiting for confirmation:

1. A slot's set fails twice (two strikes).
2. The third set lands, but the read that would confirm it fails once, so the write stays pending.
3. The user changes the PIN during that window, and the new PIN's first set fails once.
4. The slot is suspended with a `slot_suspended` repair saying it "failed after 3 consecutive attempts", though the new PIN failed only once.

When a pending write goes stale, the sync tick drops it without resetting the slot's breaker, and `request_sync_check` only asks for a reset when the slot was in sync.

Expected: strikes against a PIN that is no longer wanted don't count against the new one; the slot is suspended only after the new PIN fails the configured number of times.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Give a user a PIN on a lock whose writes fail twice, then succeed.
2. Make the confirming read after the third write fail once.
3. Change the user's PIN before the next successful read.
4. Make the first write of the new PIN fail.
5. The slot is suspended immediately.

Reproduced in the test harness while writing the regression tests in #1638.

2026.9.4

cat > 5.md <<'EOF'
### What happened?

A lock whose writes keep failing while its reads succeed is never suspended and never raises a repair, because every successful read resets the lock's failure breaker. Two cases found:

1. **Writes that hang every time.** Since #1525 a write that never returns is cut off at the operation deadline and retried, about every 10 minutes. If it hangs every time, the slot shows "syncing" forever and no repair appears. That is the "churn silently forever" outcome #1525 set out to prevent.
2. **Writes that fail as disconnected while reads succeed.** The slot is retried every sync tick (2 s) forever and never suspended, because the reads in between keep resetting the breaker the failed writes are charged to.

Expected: repeated write failures escalate (slot suspended, repair raised) even when reads keep working, so the user learns their code is not reaching the lock.

### Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Use a lock whose reads answer normally but whose writes hang (or fail as a disconnect) every time.
2. Give a Lock Code Manager user a PIN on that lock.
3. The slot stays "syncing" (or retries every 2 s) indefinitely; no `slot_suspended` or `lock_offline` repair is ever raised.

Both reproduced in the test harness while writing the regression tests in #1636 and #1638.

content.text:
I've filed the five bugs:

- **#1640** A second entry's slots stay unavailable when the lock pushes before their first read.
- **#1641** A PIN is rewritten forever when the lock re-announces Available with an empty or masked code after each set.
- **#1642** The operation after a refused write is not paced.
- **#1643** Stale strikes suspend a slot whose PIN changes while a write is pending.
- **#1644** Writes that keep failing never escalate while the lock's reads succeed. This one combines the "hangs every time" case and the "fails as disconnected" case, since both come from the same root cause.

Each issue follows the bug template, with steps to reproduce and related PRs. The catalog entries now point to the issue numbers.

**On the release notes:** yes, nearly all of these are edge cases. They involve two entries sharing one lock, a lock that answers out of order or refuses a command, or an entry whose setup failed. The current titles describe the mechanism ("don't trust a failed setup's cached config") rather than when it bites, so a list of eleven reads like eleven breakages. Leading each title with the condition fixes that.

Release-drafter builds the notes from PR titles, so retitling the merged PRs would change the notes:

| PR | Proposed title |
|---|---|
| #1623 | fix: with two entries sharing a lock, a stale lock report no longer empties the second entry's code |
| #1624 | fix(zwave_js_ui): a code the lock refuses (Supervision Fail) is reported as failed, not written |
| #1625 | fix(zwave_js): on some locks, a cleared slot no longer reads as `****` and gets cleared again (#819) |
| #1626 | fix(config_flow): adding a lock is refused when another entry already uses its slots |
| #1627 | fix(zha): a reply meant for a different command is no longer taken as the answer |
| #1629 | fix: with two entries sharing a lock, disabling or reloading one no longer stops updates for the other |
| #1630 | fix(config_flow): saving options on an entry that failed to load now reloads it |
| #1631 | fix: `hard_refresh_usercodes` accepts area and device targets |
| #1632 | fix: after an entry fails to load, entries sharing its lock no longer act on its old settings |
| #1633 | fix(sync): a lock that keeps refusing to clear a code gets a repair instead of endless retries |
| #1635 | fix: "Disable polling" applies to a lock shared by several entries |

Two more cleanups:
- **#1635's bug never shipped.** #1629 introduced it within this same release. Its new title reads as a feature rather than a regression fix, or the line could come out of the notes.
- **"Documentation" duplicates.** The test PRs #1636–#1638, plus #1627 and #1634, also show up under "Documentation". They touched `AGENTS.md`, so the file-based labeler added `documentation`. Removing that label from those five would clean up the section.

Should I apply the retitles and drop the `documentation` labels? The draft release refreshes on the next push to main, or I can regenerate it now. Going forward, I'll write fix titles in this "when it happens, then what changes" form.
yes apply retitles, dont worry about labels

## Why

1. **Module eviction:** the failure induction for the #1632 test will touch a single module only, and gets checked in isolation on a partial run.
2. **Capabilities knob:** the subagent first reads `BaseLock`. It's checking whether the capability check can run for a lock that only manages slots, the way the virtual lock does. If it can, the knob stops implying native-user support. If not, the docstring will describe the hybrid honestly.
3. **Other assertions** will check what they claim:
   - #928 captures a masked token LCM actually logged;
   - diagnostics gets round-tripped through Home Assistant's JSON encoder;
   - restarts begin from a fresh, unstarted Home Assistant where that's possible;
   - #251's second variant becomes a separate test, no longer called a regression test;
   - #1538's code check now means something;
   - the `current_entry` harness test proves no migration ran.

Round 2, the last one, comes after this, then the PR.

**From the run itself:**
- **The state-listener lead is real but latent, and #1629 didn't cause it.** After a failed setup, a lock instance can keep reacting each time the lock's integration reloads. That only happens when a push provider fails after registering its listener, and no built-in provider does that today. It behaves the same on the commit before #1629. I've logged it for the lock-handle work, since that listener belongs to the handle.
- **Two minor items are in the catalog:**
  - `hard_refresh_usercodes` succeeds silently on a lock no loaded entry manages;
  - failed reads log an empty reason.
- **#250 follows a pattern #1050 also showed:** several layers each prevent the bug on their own. That's fine for the net, which guards the outcome. For the rebuild, it shows the protection is spread out rather than owned in one place.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- `patch.dict(sys.modules)` is a quiet trap. On exit it restores the whole dict, so any module first imported inside the block gets evicted, while the parent package still holds the old object. The next import then creates a second copy of the module. The full suite hid this because test collection had already imported the module, and only a partial run exposed it.
- The #250 and #1050 results show the difference between guarding a fix and guarding an outcome. A net built to survive a core swap should guard outcomes, so it passes as long as some layer prevents the bug. That a single layer's removal goes unnoticed is something to fix in the rebuild, not in the tests.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The docstring says why it isn't the HTTP endpoint. **Re-proof:** `assert True is False`.

   - A current entry builds no extra instances, and each kept lock's first call is `setup`.
   - An old-shape entry builds 2 migration instances, one per lock, each of which only did `get_usercodes`. That shows the check can see a migration.

9. **#250:** added the docstring note that the test guards the outcome across several layered guards, for the core swap.

`-k 1632` selects nothing, because test names don't carry issue numbers, so I ran the #1632 test by its name instead.

Mutation results are in `/private/tmp/claude-501/batch3/mutation_results_round1.txt`. The scratch copy was restored after every run, and the isolation copies have been removed.</result>

**Item 1: `current_entry` detects any migration.** The test is now `test_a_current_entry_sets_up_without_a_migration[current|old_shape]` in `tests/test_harness.py`. It checks two things:
- **Version before setup:** `(entry.version == CONFIG_ENTRY_VERSION) is not migrated`.
- **Migration spy:** `patch.object(lock_code_manager, "async_migrate_entry", wraps=...)` wraps the integration's migration hook, and the test asserts `migrate.called is migrated`. HA calls that hook only when the entry needs migrating.

It still checks that no extra lock instance is built and read, that each kept lock's first call is `setup`, and that the version is current afterwards. The old-shape case shows all of these do fire on a real migration.

**Proof:** I ran your exact mutation in the scratch copy, `current_entry` built at `CONFIG_ENTRY_VERSION - 1`, restored in `finally`:
- With the full test, `[current]` fails at the version check: `assert (4 == 5) is not False`.
- With the version check also removed, the spy alone fails it: `assert True is False` on `async_migrate_entry.called`.

**Item 2: the caching claim** (the `capabilities` comment in `tests/common.py` and `AGENTS.md`).
- **Corrected claim:** BaseLock caches the first capability answer from any caller for the instance's lifetime. Allocation's slot-range ask and the write path's capacity checks keep even an answer with no PIN room. Only setup's check drops an answer that fails it.
- **When a fix is seen:** after a failed setup check, a corrected `capabilities` is seen at the lock integration's next reload only if nothing else asked in between.

**Item 3: #928 picks the record by its template.** It now matches `record.msg == "Setting usercode on %s slot %s (pin=%s, source=%s)"` with arguments `(lock.test_1, 1)`. The test asserts exactly one such record, with a message listing what it found, so a missing or duplicate log line fails clearly instead of as an unpacking error. The masked token is `args[2]`, and the line deobfuscated is that record's real message. Re-proof: with the shared data dropped on the last unload, deobfuscate raises "not fully set up".

**Item 4: deadline sizing.** The `supports_native_users` docstring, the knob comment and `AGENTS.md` now say the flag sizes each write's deadline for 3 exchanges and each clear's for one per managed slot plus one (`_base.py` around line 1566). The mock's own writes and reads stay slot-level.

## Proposed change

Batch 3a of the regression net. It covers 15 lifecycle and shared-lock bugs that were guarded only by tests asserting core internals, by partial tests, or by nothing. Those internals include `runtime_data.locks` identity, `_config_entry_state_unsub`, `_reached_once` and `_setup_succeeded`, plus tests that call `async_unload_lock` directly or patch Lock Code Manager privates to make setup fail.

Each new test goes only through Home Assistant: real config entries (setup, unload, reload, disable), the options and subentry flows, startup state changes, entity states, repairs, events, actions, diagnostics, and what the mock lock and the Z-Wave JS fake record. Failures are triggered the way they really happen:
- the lock's integration is down;
- provider setup or a read fails, through the mock lock's fault knobs;
- a platform module can't be imported, so Home Assistant's loader fails the setup.

The internals-level tests stay.

Every test fails when its fix is reverted, checked in a scratch copy:

| Bug | New test |
|---|---|
| #225 cluster | `providers/test_base.py::test_a_lock_not_connected_at_setup_gets_entities_that_come_up_with_it` |
| #247 | `test_init.py::test_an_entry_set_up_during_startup_reaches_its_lock_once_started` |
| PR #250 (sync) | `test_sync.py::test_nothing_is_set_or_cleared_before_the_lock_is_read` |
| PR #251 | `test_init.py::test_unloading_beside_a_sibling_disabled_since_startup_unloads_cleanly` |
| #865 / PR #900 | `test_init.py::test_two_entries_sharing_a_lock_at_startup_both_come_up` |
| PR #928 | `test_services.py::test_the_actions_still_answer_once_every_entry_has_unloaded` |
| #1476 / PRs #1478, #1482 | `providers/zwave_js/test_e2e.py` (one keypad notification → exactly one event) and `test_init.py::test_a_reload_beside_an_unloaded_sibling_leaves_one_push_subscription` |
| PR #1482 (part 2) | `test_init.py::test_dropping_a_lock_another_entry_manages_keeps_its_repair` |
| PR #1632 | `test_init.py::test_a_failed_entry_checks_a_lock_it_adds_against_the_users_it_saved_since` |
| PR #1048 | `providers/test_base.py::test_a_lock_whose_setup_raised_comes_up_with_its_integration` |
| #1268 (bug 2) / PR #1270 | `test_coordinator.py::test_a_lock_unread_since_startup_shows_nothing_until_it_answers` |
| #1257 / PR #1260 | `test_coordinator.py::test_a_lock_offline_since_startup_is_reported_only_once_it_was_reached` |
| #1257 / PR #1289 | `providers/test_base.py::test_a_lock_back_from_a_device_outage_gets_its_new_pin_promptly` |
| #1538 (cross-lock deletion; never reproduced, insurance) | `test_init.py::test_dropping_one_lock_leaves_the_other_locks_codes_alone` |
| PR #1344 (visible) | `providers/test_base.py::test_a_lock_failing_validation_at_setup_stays_in_the_entry_and_recovers` |

**Notes:**
- **Two tests guard the outcome rather than one specific fix:**
  - **#250 (nothing written before the first read):** several layers each prevent it, so the test fails only when all of them are removed. That is deliberate, for the core swap.
  - **#1538:** never reproduced, so this test is insurance rather than a regression test.
- **#1268 diagnostics:** the test calls the diagnostics hook and serializes the result with Home Assistant's `ExtendedJSONEncoder`, the same encoder a downloaded report uses. It doesn't go through the HTTP endpoint, because aiohttp's access log fails under the frozen clock.
- **#1632's induced failure:** the test hides only `custom_components.lock_code_manager.event`, during the failing setup (`monkeypatch.setitem`). I checked that a partial run doesn't leave a second copy of any module in the worker.

**Findings, not fixed here (recorded for the core rebuild):**
- **A latent state-listener leak.** If a push provider fails after its state listener is registered, the dropped lock keeps re-running its provider setup on every reload of the lock's integration. No built-in provider fails at that point today. Behavior is the same before #1629, so #1629 didn't introduce it.
- **A silent action.** `hard_refresh_usercodes` succeeds silently on a lock that no loaded entry manages.
- **Empty log reasons.** Failed reads log an empty reason.

**Harness additions (test-only, each with a harness test):**
- **A `capabilities` knob on `MockLCMLock`** (`PIN_CAPABILITIES` / `NO_PIN_CAPABILITIES`). Setup only checks capabilities for native-user locks, so this knob also marks the mock as one. That changes the write and clear deadlines; the mock's own reads and writes stay slot-level.
- **`current_entry(...)`** builds an entry in the current shape, so setup runs no migration. Its harness test fails if any migration runs.

**Results:**
- Full suite: 2864 passed, 3 skipped. 100% coverage on `custom_components`.
- New tests: 3 runs, all passing.
- `prek`: clean.

## Type of change

- [ ] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [x] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue:
- This PR is related to issue: #1636, #1637, #1638 (earlier batches)

Added 2026-07-31 (branch property-based-testing): `tests/properties/` (Hypothesis, runs in normal pytest; dev profile 15 examples default, `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci` → 200, wired in python-checks.yml) and `ts/pbt/` (Bombadil 0.6.1 browser harness + spec, `yarn test:pbt`, nightly bombadil.yml — never on PRs; moved from repo-root `pbt/` 2026-08-06).

Traps worth remembering:
- Hypothesis stateful + HA: per-example loop + `async_test_home_assistant` entered via `__aenter__`; teardown must `hass.async_stop(force=True)` before `__aexit__` or `verify_cleanup` explodes on leaked INSTANCES. Set `lock._min_operation_delay = 0`.
- ruff-format on py314 target ENFORCES PEP 758 unparenthesized `except TypeError, ValueError:` — don't "fix" it to parenthesized; the formatter strips it back.
- Hypothesis passed 200 examples twice before drawing `float('inf')` — a red property can be nondeterministic; triage rule: counterexample = deliverable ([[feedback-tests-with-changes]]).
- Bombadil harness must mirror SPA routing (serve harness page for extensionless paths) — cards pushState virtual HA routes and reload 404s otherwise; and any DOM text containing digits can falsely trip PIN-leak properties (rename labels are digit-free, matching uses digit-boundary regex).
- bombadil 0.6.1 ships broken .d.ts (randomRange re-export): filed antithesishq/bombadil#253; ts/pbt/tsconfig.json uses moduleResolution bundler + skipLibCheck. tsconfig.build.json must exclude `ts/pbt/**` or rollup sweeps spec.ts into the frontend build; serve.mjs derives its root from import.meta.url, so its depth matters.

## The dev profile is 15 examples — a single green run is NOT evidence

`tests/conftest.py` registers **`dev` = `max_examples=15`** (to keep the full
suite inside its seconds budget) and **`ci` = `max_examples=200`**, selected
by `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE`. Local runs default to `dev`.

On 2026-08-18 I pushed a **red** branch while reporting "1553 passed". The
pre-push run genuinely passed — 15 examples had not found the counterexample
— and later runs found and cached it in `.hypothesis`. Every green I reported
that day was 15 examples per property.

**Before pushing, always:**

```bash
rm -rf .hypothesis && HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci python -m pytest tests/ -q -p no:randomly
```

Clear the database, or a cached failure/success masks what a fresh CI run
would do. Keep `dev` for the edit loop; it is the right trade there.

Verified afterwards: `main` and `v3` are both clean at 200 examples, so

You are writing batch 3b of a regression-test net for the Lock Code Manager Home Assistant custom integration: a Hypothesis STATEFUL property machine over shared-lock lifecycle, driven only through Home Assistant surfaces. TEST-ONLY PR: no production code changes (custom_components/ untouched). If the machine finds a real bug, STOP, minimize the counterexample into a plain reproduction test saved under /private/tmp/claude-501/batch3b/ and report it; do not fix it and do not commit a failing property (you may commit the property with the failing rule excluded and a clear note, if the rest is sound).

WORKTREE (absolute paths only; never touch /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager itself or other worktrees): /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/regression-batch3b
Branch: test/regression-batch3b, STACKED on test/regression-batch3 (PR #1645, unmerged; HEAD 3b8c553b). Commit on top, do NOT push. Never run bare `git stash`. Read AGENTS.md first (it documents the regression harness built in batches 0–3a: MockLCMLock fault knobs incl. "setup"/"probe"/slow, `when_mock_lock_built`, `capabilities`, `current_entry`, records `service_calls` (incl. "setup"/"unload"), `attempt_times`, `call_order`, `noop_set_usercode`; MockLCMPushLock subscribe/unsubscribe counters; time helpers `async_advance_sync_ticks`, `async_tick_until`, `async_advance_clock`, `async_settle_background`; `LIFELONG_TASKS`). Create a venv in the worktree (`uv venv --python 3.14 && uv pip install -r requirements_dev.txt`; .venv gitignored); `yarn install` if prek's eslint needs it.

## Starting material
An earlier attempt lives on branch `refactor/lock-handle-machine` (commit af162114; worktree /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/lock-handle-machine — READ ONLY, do not modify it). See `git show af162114 -- tests/properties/test_lock_handle_machine.py tests/common.py tests/conftest.py`. It is a stateful machine over entries sharing locks (rules: set up / unload / reload / disable / enable entries, change options, etc.; invariants about one lock instance per lock, coordinator alive while held, teardown when the last holder lets go). Its review found these problems — the rebuild must fix ALL of them:
1. Dependence on internals: it asserted on `runtime_data.locks`, used `pass_lock`, patched the coordinator's shutdown, and used `async_write_entry_config` instead of the options flow. Rebuild: every rule acts through hass.config_entries (setup, unload, reload, disable/enable via async_set_disabled_by, remove) and the real options/subentry flows; every invariant is checked through surfaces: entity states (available/unavailable, in-sync), MockLCMLock records (exactly one "setup" per instance build, "unload" with (False,)/(True,), subscribe/unsubscribe balance on MockLCMPushLock, reads continuing while any loaded entry holds the lock — observe via get_usercodes calls or an out-of-band change reaching every loaded holder's in-sync entity), repairs, and the harness's `mock_lock(entry, lock_id)` identity helper where needed (that is a harness helper, not core internals; prefer behavior over identity when both work).
2. A CI time limit that masks shrinking (~24 s under coverage). Size the machine so the ci profile (HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci) finishes comfortably, set explicit `settings(max_examples=..., stateful_step_count=..., deadline=None)` for the machine, and make sure a failure SHRINKS rather than hitting a timeout first. Report wall-clock under `--cov` for dev and ci profiles.
3. An unbounded teardown that could abort the session. Teardown must be bounded and fail loudly (the memory note: stateful + HA needs a per-example hass via `async_test_home_assistant` entered with `__aenter__`, and teardown must `hass.async_stop(force=True)` before `__aexit__`, else verify_cleanup explodes on leaked instances; check how tests/properties/ does it today and follow the existing pattern). Release any held MockLCMLock faults before stopping.
4. A vacuous `coordinator is None` skip. No invariant may silently skip; if a precondition is needed, express it as a Hypothesis `precondition` on the rule, or assert.
5. Unrelated lock draws (rules drew locks that no entry used). Draw locks and entries from the machine's own model so rules target meaningful states.
6. Options rules with no checked effect. Every rule that changes config must have an observable consequence that an invariant checks (e.g. a lock dropped from all entries is unloaded permanently exactly once; a lock still held elsewhere is not; slots of the remaining entries keep their codes).
7. No concurrent boot path. Add a rule (or initialize variant) that sets up several entries sharing a lock during CoreState.starting, then fires STARTED, so the concurrent-join path is exercised (batch 3a's #865 test shows the pattern).

## Model and invariants (suggested; refine as you learn)
Model: a small set of locks (2–3) and entries (2–3); each entry's configured locks; each entry's state (loaded / not loaded / disabled). Invariants after every step (after settling with the harness helpers):
- For each lock held by at least one LOADED entry: exactly one live instance (builds minus permanent/plain unloads == 1 per lock via MockLCMLock records), and the lock is still being read / an out-of-band change reaches every loaded holder's in-sync entity within a bounded number of ticks (pick the cheaper check; must not make the machine slow).
- For each lock held by no entry: its last instance was unloaded exactly once; a push lock has subscriptions == unsubscriptions.
- An unload is permanent ((True,)) only when no enabled entry still configures that lock (PR #1482 rule).
- Every LOADED entry's slot entities exist and are not unavailable once the lock is reachable.
- No duplicate events: one lock notification → at most one event-entity change per loaded entry managing that slot (if cheap with MockLCMPushLock; otherwise skip and say so).

Each invariant must be shown to catch something: for each, introduce a mutation in a scratch rsync copy under /private/tmp/claude-501/ (restore in a `finally`) that breaks the corresponding production rule (e.g. pre-#1478 teardown "only when no other entry lists the lock", dropping `async_wait_for_setup` on join, permanent unload regardless of other entries, a failed setup leaving the instance live) and show the machine finds and shrinks it within the ci profile. Report each mutation, whether it was caught, the number of examples to find it, and the shrunk counterexample length.

Also: the latent leak found by batch 3a (a lock that fails after its state listener is registered keeps re-running its provider setup on every reload of the lock's integration; reproducible only via a push provider whose setup_push_subscription raises ProviderNotImplementedError) — if the MockLCMPushLock can raise that at subscription time with a small test-only knob, add a rule for it and an invariant ("a dropped instance never sets up again"). Expect it to FAIL on main: in that case do NOT commit it as a passing rule; keep it out of the committed machine (or behind an xfail-strict standalone test reproducing it, `@pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True, reason="latent state-listener leak; see catalog")`), and report.

Style: match tests/properties/ conventions; comments state intent, not history; spell out acronyms; no Google-style Args/Returns; no inline imports; no nonlocal/global; prefer comprehensions/next(). Note ruff-format on the py314 target enforces PEP 758 unparenthesized `except A, B:` — don't fight it.

## Verification (all before committing)
- `rm -rf .hypothesis && HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE=ci python -m pytest tests/ -q -n auto --cov --cov-report=term-missing:skip-covered`: green, 100% on custom_components. (Clear .hypothesis so cached examples don't mask a fresh CI run.)
- The machine alone 3x under the ci profile; report wall-clock with and without --cov.
- `prek run --all-files`.
Commit message: `test: a shared-lock lifecycle property machine driven through Home Assistant` + short body + trailer:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

## Report
Rules and invariants (and which earlier finding each addresses); the mutation table (mutation → caught? examples → shrunk length); timing; any real bugs found (with minimized repro paths); the latent-leak rule outcome; harness additions; suite/coverage/prek; SHA.

content.text:
Batch 3a is open as **#1645**, a test-only PR linked to this thread.

**What #1645 covers:** 15 lifecycle and shared-lock bugs, each with a test that fails when its fix is reverted. Failures are triggered the way they really happen: the lock's integration is down, a fault knob fails setup or a read, or a missing platform module makes Home Assistant's loader fail. No LCM internals are patched.

**Review:**
- Round 1 caught a real harness leak. Hiding modules with `patch.dict(sys.modules)` could leave two copies of `binary_sensor.py` loaded on a partial test run.
- Round 1 also caught several assertions that claimed more than they checked.
- Round 2 confirmed those fixes and left four small items, now fixed.

**Results:** the full suite passes (2864 tests) with 100% coverage, and `prek` is clean.

**Batch 3b** is running on `test/regression-batch3b`, stacked on #1645. It rebuilds the lock-handle property machine and fixes every problem the earlier review found:
- Each rule acts through `hass.config_entries` and the real options flow, with no internals patched.
- Each check goes through entities, the mock lock's records, and push-subscription counts.
- Teardown is bounded and fails loudly.
- The machine is sized so the CI profile can shrink a failing example before hitting the time limit.
- No check can skip silently.
- Every rule that changes config has an effect some check verifies.
- There's a concurrent-startup path.

Each check also has to be shown to catch a real past bug, such as the teardown rule from before #1478, or a missing wait when a second entry joins.

The latent state-listener leak gets a rule if the mock can trigger it cheaply. It's expected to fail on main, so it would land as a strict expected-failure test, not as a passing rule.

So a progress task that completes inside the window between core returning the progress step and the frontend's `subscribe_events` landing leaves the dialog stranded for good. A slow Z-Wave lock never loses this race; a Matter lock always does. The underlying race is arguably the frontend's: no re-fetch after subscribing. On the LCM side, a simple mitigation would be to skip `async_show_progress` when no lock in the entry needs reading, or to return the next step directly if the task is already done. ## Environment - Home Assistant 2026.10.1 (includes core#182808, the `get_lock_users` fix from #1579 / core#182526) - Lock Code Manager 6.0.1 (HACS) - Matter Server add-on 9.2.0 - Lock: Ultraloq Bolt SE over Matter/Thread, firmware 01.54.0043 — single lock in the entry ## Steps to reproduce 1. The dialog shows the `allocating` progress screen and never advances (waited 5+ minutes; reproduced twice today, including after a full HA restart and a cache-clearing hard reload). ## Evidence that the backend finished - `profiler.log_current_tasks` while the dialog was spinning: no pending task from `lock_code_manager` at all. - No `doorLock` commands from LCM in the Matter server log during the wait — expected, since allocation skips Matter locks. - `GET /api/config/config_entries/flow/` during the spin returned: `{"type": "form", "step_id": "code_slot", "description_placeholders": {"user_num": 1, "num_users": 3}, ...}` - Reloading the page and starting setup again reported the flow "already in progress" (the orphaned flow still held it). - Submitting the three `code_slot` forms by POST to the same flow ID produced `create_entry`; the entry loaded and synced all users to the lock correctly. Issue #1579 (Ultraloq Bolt SE, Matter over Thread): config flow sits on the
"reading which slots your locks already hold" spinner forever after one
`getUser(1)`. Investigated 2026-09-17.

**Refuted — do not re-derive:**

- `nextUserIndex` appears NOWHERE in Lock Code Manager. The reporter's suspected
  cause ("the slot walk follows nextUserIndex and waits on null") cannot be it.
- Allocation issues **zero** Matter reads. `credential_index_follows_slot` is
  False for Matter (`providers/matter.py`), and all three read paths in
  `domain/allocation.py` (`async_read_occupancy`, `async_check_slot_capacity`,
  `async_max_slot`) check that flag and `continue` first. Proven by test, not
  just by reading. So the `getUser(1)` in the reporter's log did NOT come from
  the step they were watching.
- **The hang did not reproduce.** Against the Matter E2E harness
  (`tests/providers/matter/conftest.py`) with `get_lock_users` returning
  `{"max_users": 10, "users": []}`: entry setup completes, and the full YAML
  config flow (select lock -> yaml -> 4 users -> allocate -> create entry ->
  setup) completes. Scratch tests were deleted; rewrite them if resuming.

**Verified mechanism for the single `getUser`:** HA core's `get_lock_users`
(`homeassistant/components/matter/lock_helpers.py`) advances ONLY by
`nextUserIndex` and breaks on null — including when read out of the all-null
response for an unoccupied index. One round trip, `users: []`, ~2s. That is also
exactly what the reporter's own `matter.get_lock_users` action returned, so the
log line may be their diagnostic call rather than ours.

**Real bug found along the way — filed upstream as home-assistant/core#182526.**
On a lock that answers `nextUserIndex: null`, HA reports an empty user table
however many users exist. Downstream consequence for us: LCM can never see its
own `lcm:{slot}:` tagged users, so it reads the lock as empty, cannot recognise
them after a restart, and never observes device-side deletions. Same family as
[[project_issue_1538_matter_multilock]].

**Two facts worth keeping:**

- HA's `ConfigEntries.async_add` schedules the storage save AFTER awaiting
  setup, so "no entry in `.storage/core.config_entries`" means setup never
  returned — it does NOT mean the entry was never created.
- HA drives its own flows past a progress task: `data_entry_flow.py` attaches a
  done-callback that re-enters `_async_configure`, and loops while the result is
  `SHOW_PROGRESS_DONE`. The frontend is a spectator, so a stalled spinner does
  not by itself implicate the browser — but the reporter separately saw a valid
  server-returned form render as a bare spinner, so the frontend is still live
  as a suspect. Related: [[feedback_dashboard_cards_cannot_use_ha_form_components]].

**Still open:** root cause of the hang. Untried avenues: real ~2s Matter
latency, unmocked `get_lock_info`, an Ultraloq-shaped node fixture. Raman chose
to file the upstream bug first and left the rest unscheduled.
